'''Esports''' ({{IPAc-en|audio=Pronunciation of "esports".ogg|'|i:|s|p|ɔːr|t|s}}), short for '''electronic sports''', is a form of competition using [[video game]]s.<ref name="whatisesports">{{cite journal |last1=Hamari |first1=Juho |last2=Sjöblom |first2=Max |date=2016 |title=What is eSports and why do people watch it? |ssrn=2686182 |journal=Internet Research |volume=27 |issue=2 |pages=211–232 |doi=10.1108/IntR-04-2016-0085|s2cid=35814803 |url=https://trepo.tuni.fi/handle/10024/101034 }}</ref> Esports often takes the form of organized, [[multiplayer video game]] competitions, particularly between professional players, played individually or as teams.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Werder |first1=Karl |title=Esport |journal=Business & Information Systems Engineering |date=June 2022 |volume=64 |issue=3 |pages=393–399 |doi=10.1007/s12599-022-00748-w|s2cid=255613366 |doi-access=free |hdl=10419/309891 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tang |first1=Di |last2=Sum |first2=Raymond Kim-wai |last3=Li |first3=Minghui |last4=Ma |first4=Ruisi |last5=Chung |first5=Peichi |last6=Ho |first6=Ray Wai-keung |title=What is esports? A systematic scoping review and concept analysis of esports |journal=[[Heliyon]] |date=2023 |volume=9 |issue=12 |article-number=e23248 |doi=10.1016/j.heliyon.2023.e23248 |pmid=38149186 |doi-access=free |pmc=10750068 |bibcode=2023Heliy...923248T }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rosell Llorens |first1=Mariona |title=eSport Gaming: The Rise of a New Sports Practice |journal=Sport, Ethics and Philosophy |date=2017 |volume=11 |issue=4 |pages=464–476 |doi=10.1080/17511321.2017.1318947}}</ref>

Multiplayer competitions were long a part of [[video game culture]], but were largely between amateurs until the late 2000s when the advent of online [[streaming media]] platforms, particularly [[YouTube]] and [[Twitch (service)|Twitch]], enabled a surge in participation by professional gamers and spectators.<ref name="2012Forbes" /><ref name="FieldOfStreams" /> By the 2010s, esports was a major part of the video game industry, with many game developers designing for and funding tournaments and other events.

Esports first became popular in [[East Asia]], particularly in [[China]] and [[South Korea]] (which first licensed professional players in 2000) but less so in [[Japan]], whose broad [[Gambling in Japan|anti-gambling laws]] prohibit professional gaming tournaments.<ref>{{cite magazine |author=Andrew Groen |date=14 May 2013 |title=Why gamers in Asia are the world's best eSport athletes |url=http://www.pcworld.com/article/2036844/why-gamers-in-asia-are-the-worlds-best-esport-athletes.html |magazine=PC World |access-date=7 October 2013}}</ref><ref name="bloomberg olympics 2024" /> Esports are also popular in [[Europe]] and the [[Americas]], which host regional and international events.

The most common [[video game genres]] associated with esports are [[multiplayer online battle arena]] (MOBA), [[first-person shooter]] (FPS), [[fighting game]]s, [[Digital collectible card game|card]], [[Battle royale game|battle royales]], and [[real-time strategy]] (RTS) games. Popular esports franchises include ''[[League of Legends]]'', ''[[Dota]]'', ''[[Counter-Strike]]'', ''[[Valorant]]'', ''[[Overwatch (video game)|Overwatch]]'', ''[[Street Fighter]]'', ''[[Super Smash Bros.]]'' and ''[[StarCraft]]''. Among the most popular tournaments are the [[League of Legends World Championship|''League of Legends'' World Championship]], [[The International (Dota 2)|''Dota 2''{{'s}} International]], the fighting game-specific [[Evolution Championship Series]] (EVO) and [[Intel Extreme Masters]]. Many other competitions use a series of league play with sponsored teams, such as the [[Overwatch League]]. Although the legitimacy of esports as a true sporting competition remains in question, they have been featured alongside traditional sports in some multinational events in Asia. The [[International Olympic Committee]] has discussed their inclusion in future Olympic events, starting with the [[Olympic Esports Games]] set to be held in 2027.

In the early 2010s, viewership was about 85% male and 15% female, with most viewers between the ages of 18 and 34.<ref>{{cite web |date=14 November 2012 |title=Major League Gaming reports COWS GO MOO 334 percent growth in live video |url=http://www.gamespot.com/news/major-league-gaming-reports-334-percent-growth-in-live-video-6400010 |access-date=8 October 2013 |website=[[GameSpot]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |author=John Gaudiosi |date=28 April 2012 |title=Team Evil Geniuses Manager Anna Prosser Believes More Female Gamers Will Turn Pro |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/johngaudiosi/2012/04/28/team-evil-geniuses-manager-anna-prosser-believes-more-female-gamers-will-turn-pro/ |magazine=Forbes |access-date=8 October 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |author=John Gaudiosi |date=29 July 2012 |title=Taipei Assassins Manager Erica Tseng Talks Growth Of Female Gamers In League Of Legends |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/johngaudiosi/2012/07/29/taipei-assassins-manager-erica-tseng-talks-growth-of-female-gamers-in-league-of-legends/ |access-date=8 October 2013 |work=Forbes}}</ref> By the late 2010s, it was estimated that by 2020, the total audience of esports would grow to 454 million viewers, with revenue increasing to more than {{USD}}1 billion, with China accounting for 35% of the global esports revenue.<ref>{{cite web|website=[[VentureBeat]]|url=https://venturebeat.com/2020/02/25/newzoo-global-esports-will-top-1-billion-in-2020-with-china-as-the-top-market/|title=Newzoo: Global esports will top $1 billion in 2020, with China as the top market|date=25 February 2020|access-date=6 November 2021|archive-date=2 August 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220802165919/https://venturebeat.com/2020/02/25/newzoo-global-esports-will-top-1-billion-in-2020-with-china-as-the-top-market/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-videogames-outlook-idUSKCN1Q11XY|title=Global esports revenues to top $1 billion in 2019: report|date=12 February 2019|work=Reuters|access-date=21 May 2019|language=en}}</ref>

==History==

===Early history (1972–1989)===
[[File:Space Invaders Championship.jpg|thumb|left|Attendees of the 1981 ''[[Space Invaders]]'' Championships attempt to set the highest score.]]

The earliest known video game competition took place on 19 October 1972 at [[Stanford University]] for the game ''[[Spacewar!]]'' Stanford students were invited to an "Intergalactic spacewar olympics" whose grand prize was a year's subscription for ''[[Rolling Stone]]'', with Bruce Baumgart winning the five-man-free-for-all tournament, and Slim Tovar and Robert E. Maas winning the team competition.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kotaku.com/today-is-the-40th-anniversary-of-the-worlds-first-known-5953371 |title=Today is the 40th Anniversary of the World's First Known Video Gaming Tournament |author=Owen Good |publisher=Kotaku |date=19 October 2012 |access-date=1 August 2013}}</ref>

Contemporary esports has roots in competitive face-to-face [[arcade video game]] competitions. A forerunner of esports was held by [[Sega]] in 1974, the All Japan TV Game Championships, a nationwide arcade video game tournament in Japan.<ref name="VT">{{cite magazine |title=Sega Sponsors All Japan TV Game Championships |magazine=[[Vending Times]] |date=December 1974 |url=https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E13XZPWVgAEzeJH?format=png |access-date=26 September 2021 |archive-date=8 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230308205711/https://pbs.twimg.com/media/E13XZPWVgAEzeJH?format=png |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Borowy">{{cite journal |last1=Borowy |first1=Michael |last2=Jin |first2=Dal Yong |last3=Pluda |first3=Alessandra |title=Pioneering eSport: The Experience Economy and the Marketing of Early 1980s Arcade Gaming Contests |journal=[[International Journal of Communication]] |date=15 October 2013 |volume=7 |pages=1–21 (9) |issn=1932-8036 |url=https://ijoc.org/index.php/ijoc/article/viewFile/2296/999#page=9}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Zhouxiang |first1=Lu |chapter=Competitive Gaming |editor-last1=Phillips |editor-first1=Murray G. |editor-last2=Booth |editor-first2=Douglas |editor-last3=Adams |editor-first3=Carly |title=Routledge Handbook of Sport History |date=19 September 2021 |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-1-000-44166-6 |page=337 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eBo6EAAAQBAJ&pg=PT337}}</ref> The tournament was intended by Sega to promote the play and sales of video games in the country. There were local tournaments held in 300 locations across Japan, and then sixteen finalists from across the country competed in the final elimination rounds at [[Tokyo]]'s Hotel Pacific. Prizes awarded included [[television sets]] ([[Color television|color]] and [[black-and-white]]), [[cassette tape recorder]]s and [[transistor radios]]. According to Sega, the tournament "proved to be the biggest event ever" in the [[arcade game]] industry, and was attended by members from leading [[Japanese newspapers]] and [[leisure industry]] companies.<ref name="VT"/> Sega stressed "the importance of such tournaments to foster better business relationships between the maker-location-customer and create an atmosphere of competition on TV amusement games".<ref name="Borowy"/><ref name="VT"/> In 1977, [[Gremlin Industries]] (a year before being acquired by Sega) held a marketing stunt to promote their early arcade [[Snake (video game genre)|snake game]] ''Hustle'' in the United States, involving the "Gremlin Girls" who were a duo of professional [[Women and video games|female arcade players]] called Sabrina Osment and Lynn Reid.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Johnson |first1=Ethan |title=The Sega-Gremlin Marketing Video Archive: Nearly a decade before they did what Nintendon't, Sega's marketing still managed to break new ground…even when it was really cheesy |url=https://gamehistory.org/sega-gremlin-archive/ |access-date=26 September 2021 |work=Video Game History Foundation |date=16 November 2018}}</ref><ref name="girlboss">{{cite news |last1=Drewis |first1=Deena |title=The Little-Known Female Duo That Obliterated The Gaming Scene In The '70s |url=https://www.girlboss.com/read/2018-3-14-gremlin-girls-history |access-date=26 September 2021 |work=Girlboss |date=15 March 2018}}</ref> The pair travelled across 19 American cities, where players could challenge them in [[best-of-three]] matches for a chance to win money. The duo were challenged by a total of 1,300 players, only about seven of whom managed to beat them.<ref name="girlboss"/>

The [[golden age of arcade video games]] was heralded by [[Taito]]'s ''[[Space Invaders]]'' in 1978, which popularized the use of a persistent [[high score]] for all players. Several video games in the next several years followed suit, adding other means of tracking high scores such with high score tables that included the players' initials in games like ''[[Asteroids (video game)|Asteroids]]'' in 1979. High score-chasing became a popular activity and a means of competition.<ref name="goldenage arcade esports">{{cite journal | title = Pioneering E-Sport: The Experience Economy and the Marketing of Early 1980s Arcade Gaming Contests | first1 = Michael | last1 = Borowy | first2 = Dal Yong | last2 = Jin | journal = International Journal of Communication | volume = 7 | date = 2013 | pages = 2254–2274 | issn = 1932-8036 }}</ref> The [[Space Invaders#In popular culture|Space Invaders Championship]] held by [[Atari]] in 1980 was the earliest large scale video game competition, attracting more than 10,000 participants across the United States, establishing competitive gaming as a mainstream hobby.<ref name="eg_2_36">{{cite journal |title=Players Guide To Electronic Science Fiction Games |journal=[[Electronic Games]] |date=March 1982 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=35–45 [36] |url=https://archive.org/stream/electronic-games-magazine-1982-03/Electronic_Games_Issue_02_Vol_01_02_1982_Mar#page/n35/mode/1up |access-date=1 February 2012}}</ref> It was won by [[Rebecca Heineman]].<ref name="Women in Gaming">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3ad2DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA32 |title=Women in Gaming: 100 Professionals of Play |first=Meagan |last=Marie |date=4 December 2018 |publisher=[[Dorling Kindersley]] |isbn=978-0-241-39506-6 |pages=32–33}}</ref> [[Walter Day]], owner of an arcade in Iowa, had taken it upon himself to travel across the United States to record the high scores on various games in 1980, and on his return, founded [[Twin Galaxies]], a high score record-keeping organization.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/walter-day-leaves-twin-galaxies |title=Walter Day leaves Twin Galaxies |date=8 March 2010 |access-date=18 September 2013 |first=Tom |last=Bramwell |work=EuroGamer}}</ref> The organization went on to help promote video games and publicize its records through publications such as the ''[[Guinness World Records|Guinness Book of World Records]]'', and in 1983 it created the [[U.S. National Video Game Team]]. The team was involved in competitions, such as running the [[Video Game Masters Tournament]] for ''Guinness World Records''<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamesetwatch.com/2006/10/worlds_oldest_competitive_game_1.php |title=World's Oldest Competitive Gamer Passes On |date=20 October 2006 |access-date=18 September 2013 |first=Simon |last=Carless |work=[[GameSetWatch]] |archive-date=28 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170628033509/http://www.gamesetwatch.com/2006/10/worlds_oldest_competitive_game_1.php }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamesetwatch.com/2009/05/walter_day_twin_galaxies_and_t.php |title=Walter Day: Twin Galaxies and the Two Golden Domes |date=4 May 2009 |access-date=18 September 2013 |work=GameSetWatch |first=Eric |last=Caoili |archive-date=5 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305192749/http://www.gamesetwatch.com/2009/05/walter_day_twin_galaxies_and_t.php }}</ref> and sponsoring the North American Video Game Challenge tournament.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1454&dat=19841223&id=gbUsAAAAIBAJ&pg=4902,2359808 |title=Video champ tourney bound |date=23 December 1984 |access-date=20 September 2013 |newspaper=Sunday Star-News |page=6F}}</ref> A multicity tour in 1983, the "Electronic Circus", was used to feature these players in live challenges before audiences, and draw more people to video games.<ref name="goldenage arcade esports"/> These video game players and tournaments were featured in well-circulated newspapers and popular magazines including ''[[Life (magazine)|Life]]'' and ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' and became minor celebrities at the time, such as [[Billy Mitchell (gamer)|Billy Mitchell]].<ref>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080229043301/http://www.oxfordamericanmag.com/content.cfm?ArticleID=58&Entry=Home |archive-date=29 February 2008 |url=http://www.oxfordamericanmag.com/content.cfm?ArticleID=58&Entry=Home |first=David |last=Ramsey |work=[[Oxford American]] |title=The Perfect Man: How Billy Mitchell became a video-game superstar and achieved Pac-Man bliss.}}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis |title=Public Gaming: eSport and Event Marketing in the Experience Economy |chapter-url=http://summit.sfu.ca/system/files/iritems1/12463/etd7439_MBorowy.pdf |author=Michael Borowy |chapter=3 |year=2012 |access-date=18 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140106033104/http://summit.sfu.ca/system/files/iritems1/12463/etd7439_MBorowy.pdf |archive-date=6 January 2014 |url-status=live }}</ref> Besides establishing the competitive nature of games, these types of promotional events all formed the nature of the marketing and promotion that formed the basis of modern esports.<ref name="goldenage arcade esports"/>

In 1984, [[Konami]] and [[Centuri]] jointly held an international ''[[Track & Field (video game)|Track & Field]]'' arcade game competition that drew more than a million players from across Japan and North America. ''[[Play Meter]]'' in 1984 called it "the coin-op event of the year" and an "event on a scale never before achieved in the industry".<ref name="Sharpe">{{cite magazine |last=Sharpe |first=Roger C. |title=1984—Every Which Way But Up |magazine=[[Play Meter]] |date=December 1984 |volume=10 |issue=23 |pages=39, 49–51 |url=https://archive.org/details/play-meter-volume-10-number-23-december-15th-1984/Play%20Meter%20-%20Volume%2010%2C%20Number%2023%20-%20December%2015th%201984/page/49}}</ref> {{As of|2016}}, it holds the record for the largest organized video game competition of all time, according to ''[[Guinness World Records]]''.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Baker |first1=Chris |title=How 'Track & Field' Launched World's Biggest Video Game Tournament |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/culture/culture-news/how-konamis-track-field-launched-worlds-biggest-game-tournament-103592/ |access-date=6 October 2021 |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |date=16 August 2016}}</ref>

Televised esports events aired during this period included the American show ''[[Starcade]]'' which ran from 1982 to 1984 airing a total of 133 episodes, on which contestants would attempt to beat each other's high scores on an arcade game.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kotaku.com/arcades-dont-make-for-good-tv-but-starcades-do-5811611 |title=Arcades Don't Make for Good TV (But Starcades do) |date=14 June 2011 |access-date=17 September 2013 |work=Kotaku |first=Luke |last=Plunkett}}</ref> A video game tournament was included as part of TV show ''[[That's Incredible!]]'',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://techcrunch.com/2009/07/29/the-thats-incredible-video-game-invitational-this-is-what-we-used-to-watch/ |title=The That's Incredible! Video Game Invitational: This is what we used to watch |date=29 July 2009 |access-date=30 September 2013 |first=John |last=Biggs |work=Tech Crunch}}</ref> and tournaments were also featured as part of the plot of various films, including 1982's ''[[Tron]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/tron-1982 |title=TRON |date=1 January 1982 |access-date=20 September 2013 |first=Roger |last=Ebert}}</ref> In the UK, the [[BBC]] game show ''[[First Class (game show)|First Class]]'' included competitive video game rounds featuring the contemporary arcade games, such as ''[[Hyper Sports]]'', ''[[720°]]'' and ''[[Paperboy (video game)|Paperboy]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=First Class |url=http://www.tvcream.co.uk/telly/tv-a-z/a-m/f-is-for/first-class/ |website=TV Cream |date=May 2009 |access-date=14 June 2018 }}{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Weaver |first1=Iain |title=Weaver's Week 2012-08-12: First Class |url=http://www.ukgameshows.com/ukgs/Weaver%27s_Week_2012-08-12 |website=UK Gameshows.com |publisher=Labyrinth Games |access-date=14 June 2018}}</ref> In the United States, the Amusement Players Association held its first [[U.S. National Video Game Team]] competition in January 1987, where ''[[Vs. Super Mario Bros.]]'' was popular among competitive arcade players.<ref name="Horowitz">{{cite book |last1=Horowitz |first1=Ken |title=Beyond Donkey Kong: A History of Nintendo Arcade Games |date=30 July 2020 |publisher=[[McFarland & Company]] |isbn=978-1-4766-4176-8 |page=156 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UXD0DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA156}}</ref>

The 1988 game ''[[Netrek]]'' was an [[Internet game]] for up to 16 players, written almost entirely in [[cross-platform]] [[open source software|open-source software]]. ''Netrek'' was the [[History of online games|third Internet game]], the first Internet game to use metaservers to locate open game servers, and the first to have persistent [[user information]]. In 1993 it was credited by ''[[Wired Magazine]]'' as "the first online sports game".<ref>{{cite magazine |author=Kevin Kelly |url=https://www.wired.com/wired/archive/1.06/netrek.html |title=The First Online Sports Game |magazine=Wired |publisher=wired.com |date=Dec 1993 |access-date=1 July 2013}}</ref>

===Growth and online video games (1990–1999)===
[[File:QuakeCon 1996 - 31.jpg|thumb|Players competing at the first [[QuakeCon]] in 1996]]
The [[fighting game]] ''[[Street Fighter II]]'' (1991) popularized the concept of direct, tournament-level competition between two players.<ref name="egm_influential_sf2">{{cite magazine|last=Patterson|first=Eric L.|title=EGM Feature: The 5 Most Influential Japanese Games Day Four: Street Fighter II|url=http://www.egmnow.com/articles/news/egm-featurethe-5-most-influential-japanese-gamesday-four-street-fighter-ii/|magazine=[[Electronic Gaming Monthly]]|access-date=17 April 2012|date=3 November 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170314064721/http://www.egmnow.com/articles/news/egm-featurethe-5-most-influential-japanese-gamesday-four-street-fighter-ii/|archive-date=14 March 2017}}</ref> Previously, video games most often relied on [[high score]]s to determine the best player, but this changed with ''Street Fighter II'', where players would instead challenge each other directly, "face-to-face", to determine the best player,<ref name="egm_influential_sf2"/> paving the way for the competitive [[Multiplayer video game|multiplayer]] and [[Deathmatch (gaming)|deathmatch]] modes found in modern [[action game]]s.<ref name="barton_sf2">{{cite book|title=Vintage games: an insider look at the history of Grand Theft Auto, Super Mario, and the most influential games of all time|year=2009|publisher=Focal Press/Elsevier|location=Boston|isbn=978-0-240-81146-8|pages=239–255|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=M_bFdsP9L7oC|author=Matt Barton|author2=Bill Loguidice |access-date=17 April 2012}}</ref> The popularity of fighting games such as ''[[Street Fighter]]'' and ''[[Marvel vs. Capcom]]'' in the 1990s led to the foundation of the international [[Evolution Championship Series]] (EVO) esports tournament in 1996.

Large esports tournaments in the 1990s include the 1990 [[Nintendo World Championships]], which toured across the United States, and held its finals at [[Universal Studios Hollywood]] in California. [[Nintendo]] held a 2nd World Championships in 1994 for the [[Super Nintendo Entertainment System]] called the [[Nintendo PowerFest '94]]. There were 132 finalists that played in the finals in [[San Diego]], California. Mike Iarossi took home 1st prize. [[Blockbuster Video]] also ran their own World Game Championships in the early 1990s, co-hosted by ''[[GamePro]]'' magazine. Citizens from the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Chile were eligible to compete. Games from the 1994 championships included ''[[NBA Jam (1993 video game)|NBA Jam]]'' and ''[[Virtua Racing]]''.<ref>{{Citation |title=Blockbuster Video World Game Championship Guide |publisher=GamePro Magazine |date=June 1994 |url=https://www.flickr.com/photos/lampbane/150765934/}}</ref>

Television shows featuring esports during this period include the British shows ''[[GamesMaster]]'' and ''[[Bad Influence!]]''; the Australian game show ''[[A*mazing]]'', where in the final round contestants competed in a video game face-off; and the Canadian game show ''[[Video & Arcade Top 10]]''.

In the 1990s, many games benefited from increasing [[internet connectivity]], especially [[PC game]]s. Inspired by the fighting games ''Street Fighter II'', ''[[Fatal Fury]]'' and ''[[Art of Fighting]]'', [[id Software]]'s [[John Romero]] established competitive multiplayer in [[online games]] with ''[[Doom (1993 video game)|Doom]]''{{'}}s deathmatch mode in 1993.<ref>{{cite book|last=Consalvo|first=Mia|year=2016|title=Atari to Zelda: Japan's Videogames in Global Contexts|pages=201–3|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tH3TCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA201|publisher=[[MIT Press]]|isbn=978-0-262-03439-5}}</ref> Tournaments established in the late 1990s include the [[Cyberathlete Professional League]] (CPL), [[QuakeCon]], and the [[Professional Gamers League]]. PC games played at the CPL included the ''[[Counter-Strike (series)|Counter-Strike]]'' series, ''[[Quake series|Quake]]'' series, ''[[StarCraft (video game)|StarCraft]]'', and ''[[Warcraft (series)|Warcraft]]''.

===Global tournaments (2000–present)===
[[File:LOL2016WorldsFinalsArena.jpg|thumb|The [[League of Legends World Championship]] is an annual ''[[League of Legends]]'' tournament that rotates its venues around the world.]]
The growth of esports in South Korea is thought to have been influenced by the mass building of [[broadband Internet]] networks following the [[1997 Asian financial crisis]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/10/20/technology/league-of-legends-south-korea-epicenter-esports.html?_r=0 |title=For South Korea, E-Sports Is National Pastime |last=Mozur |first=Paul |website=[[The New York Times]] |date=19 October 2014 |access-date=13 June 2015}}</ref> It is also thought that the high [[unemployment rate]] at the time caused many people to look for things to do while out of work.<ref>{{cite book |title=Korea's Online Gaming Empire |first=Dal Yong |last=Jin |publisher=[[MIT Press]] |year=2010}}</ref> Instrumental to this growth of esports in South Korea was the prevalence of the Komany-style [[internet café]]/[[LAN gaming center]], known as a [[PC bang]]. The [[Korean e-Sports Association]], an arm of the [[Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism (South Korea)|Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism]], was founded in 2000 to promote and regulate esports in the country.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.e-sports.or.kr/board.php?b_no=9&_module=kespa&_page=view&b_no=9&b_pid=9999989400 |title=History of Korea e-Sports Association 1999–2004 |publisher=KeSPA |access-date=7 October 2013 |language=ko}}</ref> Minister of Culture, Sports, and Tourism [[Park Jie-won]] coined the term "Esports" at the founding ceremony of the 21st Century Professional Game Association (currently [[Korean e-Sports Association]]) in 2000.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jin |first1=Dal-yong |date=19 June 2020 |title=Historiography of Korean Esports: Perspectives on Spectatorship. |url=https://ijoc.org/index.php/ijoc/article/view/13795 |journal=International Journal of Communication |volume=14 |page=19 |issn=1932-8036 |access-date=23 August 2021 }}</ref>

"[[Evo Moment 37]]", also known as the "Daigo Parry", refers to a portion of a ''[[Street Fighter III: 3rd Strike]]'' semi-final match held at [[Evolution Championship Series 2004]] (Evo 2004) between [[Daigo Umehara]] (playing [[Ken Masters]]) and [[Justin Wong]] (playing [[Chun-Li]]). During this match, Umehara made an unexpected [[Comeback (sports)|comeback]] by parrying 15 consecutive hits of Wong's "Super Art" move while having only one pixel of [[health (gaming)|vitality]]. Umehara subsequently won the match. "Evo Moment #37" is frequently described as the most iconic and memorable moment in the history of competitive video gaming. Being at one point the most-watched competitive gaming moment of all time, it has been compared to sports moments such as [[Babe Ruth's called shot]] and the [[Miracle on Ice]].<ref name=KotakuBook>{{cite web|url=https://kotaku.com/someone-wrote-a-book-about-street-fighters-greatest-mat-1563009143|work=[[Kotaku]]|title=Someone Wrote A Book About Street Fighter's Greatest Match|last=Narcisse|first=Evan|date=14 April 2014}}</ref>

In April 2006, the [[G7 teams]] federation were formed by seven prominent ''[[Counter-Strike]]'' teams. The goal of the organization was to increase stability in the esports world, particularly in standardizing player transfers and working with leagues and organizations. The founding members were [[4Kings]], [[Fnatic]], [[Made in Brazil (esports)|Made in Brazil]], [[Mousesports]], [[NiP]], [[SK-Gaming]], and [[Team 3D (esports)|Team 3D]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.fnatic.com/content/1155 |title=G7 teams launched |author=G7 Federation |date=20 April 2006 |website=[[Fnatic]] |access-date=12 June 2015 |archive-date=23 December 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161223211219/http://www.fnatic.com/content/1155 }}</ref> The organization only lasted until 2009 before dissolving.<ref name="raising">{{cite book |title=Raising the Stakes: E-Sports and the Professionalization |first=TL |last=Taylor |year=2013}}</ref>

The 2000s was a popular time for televised esports. Television coverage was best established in South Korea, with ''[[StarCraft]]'' and ''[[Warcraft III]]'' competitions regularly televised by dedicated 24-hour cable TV game channels [[Ongamenet]] and [[MBCGame]].<ref name="autogenerated3">{{cite web |url=http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/c/a/2007/06/11/BUG8SQC59E1.DTL |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081007204410/http://www.sfgate.com/cgi-bin/article.cgi?f=/c/a/2007/06/11/BUG8SQC59E1.DTL |url-status=dead |archive-date=7 October 2008 |title=League beginning for video gamers |publisher=Sfgate.com |date=11 June 2007 |access-date=4 June 2012 |first=Ryan |last=Kim}}</ref> Elsewhere, esports television coverage was sporadic. The [[Television in Germany|German]] [[GIGA Television]] covered esports until its shutdown in 2009. The United Kingdom [[satellite television]] channel [[XLEAGUE.TV]] broadcast esports competitions from 2007 to 2009. The online esports only channel ESL TV<ref>{{cite web |url=http://tv.esl.eu/de/ |title=ESL TV |access-date=16 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120504091912/http://tv.esl.eu/de/ |archive-date=4 May 2012 }}</ref> briefly attempted a paid television model renamed GIGA II from June 2006 to autumn 2007. The [[Television in France|French]] channel [[Game One]] broadcast esports matches in a show called ''Arena Online'' for the [[Xfire]] Trophy.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.sk-gaming.com/video/1821-Xfire_Trophy_CC3__Arena_Online_on_Gameone_TV |title=Xfire Trophy CC3 @ Arena Online on Gameone TV |website=SK Gaming |access-date=17 September 2013 |archive-date=4 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171104132548/http://www.sk-gaming.com/video/1821-Xfire_Trophy_CC3__Arena_Online_on_Gameone_TV }}</ref> The United States channel [[ESPN2]] hosted ''[[Madden NFL]]'' competitions in a show called ''[[Madden Nation]]'' from 2005 to 2008.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.operationsports.com/news/269002/espn2s-madden-nation-to-begin-fourth-season/ |title=ESPN2's Madden Nation to Begin Fourth Season |publisher=Operation Sports |author=Steve_OS |date=15 September 2008 |access-date=16 September 2013 |archive-date=3 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131203001015/http://www.operationsports.com/news/269002/espn2s-madden-nation-to-begin-fourth-season/ }}</ref> [[DirecTV]] broadcast the [[Championship Gaming Series]] tournament for two seasons in 2007 and 2008.<ref name=autogenerated3 /> [[CBS]] aired prerecorded footage of the 2007 [[World Series of Video Games]] tournament that was held in [[Louisville, Kentucky]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/07/28/arts/television/28vide.html |work=The New York Times |first=Seth |last=Schiesel |title=Video Game Matches to Be Televised on CBS |date=28 July 2007 |access-date=4 December 2013}}</ref> The [[G4 (U.S. TV channel)|G4 television channel]] originally covered video games exclusively, but broadened its scope to cover technology and men's lifestyle, though has now shutdown.<ref name=autogenerated3 />

During the 2010s, esports grew tremendously, incurring a large increase in both viewership and prize money.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=2011: The Year of eSports |magazine=PCWorld |url=http://www.pcworld.com/article/214432/2011_the_year_of_esports.html |date=29 December 2010 |author=Patrick Miller |access-date=15 August 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/sns-201402121100--tms--invideogctnzs-c20140212-20140212,0,643102.story |title='Ender's Game' Blu-ray gets ESports tournament |date=12 February 2014 |access-date=20 February 2014 |first=John |last=Gaudiosi |work=Chicago Tribune |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140226233042/http://www.chicagotribune.com/entertainment/sns-201402121100--tms--invideogctnzs-c20140212-20140212,0,643102.story |archive-date=26 February 2014 }}</ref> Although large tournaments were founded before the 21st century, the number and scope of tournaments has increased significantly, going from about 10 tournaments in 2000 to about 260 in 2010.<ref name="FieldOfStreams">{{cite web |url=https://www.theverge.com/2013/9/30/4719766/twitch-raises-20-million-esports-market-booming |title=Field of Streams: How Twitch Made Video Games a Spectator Sport |work=The Verge |author=Ben Popper |date=30 September 2013 |access-date=9 October 2013}}</ref> Many successful tournaments were founded during this period, including the [[World Cyber Games]], the [[Intel Extreme Masters]], and [[Major League Gaming]]. The proliferation of tournaments included experimentation with competitions outside traditional esports genres. For example, the September 2006 [[FUN Technologies]] Worldwide Webgames Championship featured 71 contestants competing in [[casual games]] for a $1 million grand prize.<ref>{{cite web |title=Casual gamer gets serious prize |author=Tim Surette |work =GameSpot |date=11 September 2006 |url=http://www.gamespot.com/pc/puzzle/zumadeluxe/news.html?sid=6157427}}</ref>

The popularity and emergence of [[streaming media|online streaming services]] have helped the growth of esports in this period, and are the most common method of watching tournaments. [[Twitch (service)|Twitch]], an online streaming platform launched in 2011, routinely streams popular esports competitions. In 2013, viewers of the platform watched 12 billion minutes of video on the service, with the two most popular Twitch broadcasters being ''[[League of Legends]]'' and ''[[Dota 2]]''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailydot.com/esports/twitch-growth-esports-streaming-mlg-youtube-2013/ |title=Twitch dominated streaming in 2013, and here are the numbers to prove it |work=The Daily Dot |author=Patrick Howell O'Neill |date=16 January 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref> During one day of The International, Twitch recorded 4.5 million unique views, with each viewer watching for an average of two hours.<ref name=FieldOfStreams/>

The modern esports boom has also seen a rise in video games companies embracing the esports potential of their products. After many years of ignoring and at times suppressing the esports scene, [[Nintendo]] hosted Wii Games Summer 2010. Spanning over a month, the tournament had over 400,000 participants, making it the largest and most expansive tournament in the company's history. In 2014 Nintendo hosted an invitational ''[[Super Smash Bros. for Wii U]]'' competitive tournament at the [[E3 2014|2014]] [[Electronic Entertainment Expo]] (E3) press conference that was streamed online on Twitch.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.esportsmax.com/news/nintendo-announces-super-smash-bros-invitational-e3-2014 |title=Nintendo Announces Super Smash Bros. Invitational at E3 2014 |publisher=eSports Max |author=Alex R |work=eSportsMax |date=29 April 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141109220611/http://www.esportsmax.com/news/nintendo-announces-super-smash-bros-invitational-e3-2014 |archive-date=9 November 2014 }}</ref> [[Halo (series)|Halo]] developers [[343 Industries]] announced in 2014 plans to revive Halo as an esport with the creation of the [[Halo Championship Series]] and a prize pool of US$50,000.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://gamerant.com/halo-championship-series-esports-league/ |title=Microsoft Launching 'Halo Championship Series' eSports League |publisher=Game Rant |author=Jasmine Henry |date=7 September 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref> Both [[Blizzard Entertainment]] and [[Riot Games]] have their own [[college sports|collegiate]] outreach programs with their North American Collegiate Championship.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://na.lolesports.com/articles/announcing-north-american-collegiate-championship |title=Announcing the North American Collegiate Championship |publisher=Riot Games |author=Steve ''Jaws'' Jaworski |date=1 July 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014 |archive-date=16 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150916083616/http://na.lolesports.com/articles/announcing-north-american-collegiate-championship |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/blizzard-esports-initiative-will-support-your-college-gaming-club/1100-6417615/ |title=Blizzard eSports initiative will support your college gaming club |publisher=GameSpot |author=Emanuel Maiberg |date=8 February 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref> Since 2013 universities and colleges in the United States such as [[Robert Morris University Illinois]] and the [[University of Pikeville]] have recognized esports players as [[varsity team|varsity]] level athletes and offer [[athletic scholarship]]s.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Tassi |first1=Paul |title=Second US College Now Offering 'League of Legends' Scholarship |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/insertcoin/2015/01/08/second-us-college-now-offering-league-of-legends-scholarship/ |website=www.forbes.com |access-date=22 February 2015}}</ref> In 2017, [[Tespa]], Blizzard Entertainment's collegiate esports division, unveiled its new initiative to provide scholarships and prizes for collegiate esports clubs competing in its tournaments worth US$1 million.<ref>{{Cite news |url=http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/20360800/tespa-expand-collegiate-esports-1-million-scholarships-prizes |title=Tespa to expand collegiate esports with $1 million in scholarships and prizes |work=ESPN.com|access-date=21 September 2017}}</ref> Colleges have begun granting scholarships to students who qualify to play esports professionally for the school. Colleges such as [[Columbia College (Missouri)|Columbia College]], [[Robert Morris University Illinois|Robert Morris University]], and [[Indiana Institute of Technology]] have taken part in this.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/21152905/college-esports-list-varsity-esports-programs-north-america|title=List of varsity esports programs spans North America|work=ESPN.com|access-date=10 May 2018}}</ref> In 2018, [[Harrisburg University of Science and Technology]] began a tuition scholarship program for esports players.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/23340396/harrisburg-university-hosts-international-tryout-esports-scholarships|title=Harrisburg University hosts international esports tryout|work=ESPN.com|access-date=14 May 2018}}</ref>

[[File:Froskurinn at All Star 2017.jpg|thumb|right|Esports commentator [[Froskurinn]] in 2017]]
In 2014, the largest independent esports league, [[Electronic Sports League]], partnered with the local brand Japan Competitive Gaming to try and grow esports in the country.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.turtle-entertainment.com/news/esl-to-bring-world-class-esports-to-japan-with-new-local-partner/ |title=ESL to bring world class eSports to Japan with new local partner |date=4 September 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref>

Physical viewership of esports competitions and the scope of events have increased in tandem with the growth of online viewership.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/insertcoin/2014/09/07/espn-boss-declares-esports-not-a-sport/#55948bb5f80a |title=ESPN Boss Declares eSports 'Not A Sport' |last1=Tassi |first1=Paul |magazine=[[Forbes]] |access-date=15 December 2017 }}</ref> In 2013, the [[Season 3 League of Legends World Championship]] was held in a sold-out [[Staples Center]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://na.leagueoflegends.com/en/news/esports/esports-editorial/one-world-championship-32-million-viewers |title=One World Championship, 32 million viewers |access-date=2 September 2015 |archive-date=2 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180102050548/https://na.leagueoflegends.com/en/news/esports/esports-editorial/one-world-championship-32-million-viewers }}</ref> The [[2014 League of Legends World Championship]] in [[Seoul]], South Korea, had over 40,000 fans in attendance and featured the band [[Imagine Dragons]], and opening and closing ceremonies in addition to the competition.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Magrino |first1=Tom |title=Welcome to the League of Legends 2014 World Championship! |url=http://na.lolesports.com/articles/league-legends-world-championship-2014 |access-date=20 August 2014 |archive-date=23 September 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923045828/http://na.lolesports.com/articles/league-legends-world-championship-2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2015, the first Esports Arena was launched in [[Santa Ana, California]], as the United States' first dedicated esports facility.<ref>[https://venturebeat.com/2017/04/11/las-vegas-will-get-its-own-esports-arena-at-the-luxor-hotel/ Esports arena is coming to the Luxor Hotel in Las Vegas] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171003030944/https://venturebeat.com/2017/04/11/las-vegas-will-get-its-own-esports-arena-at-the-luxor-hotel/ |date=3 October 2017 }} Retrieved 2 October 2017</ref>

The global esports audience reached 662.6 million in 2020, and 921 million in 2022.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chiovato |first1=Luca |title=Gaming's Live-Streaming Audience Will Hit One Billion Next Year & 1.4 Billion by 2025 |url= https://newzoo.com/resources/blog/gamings-live-streaming-audience-will-hit-one-billion-next-year-1-4-billion-by-2025 |website=Newzoo |date=6 May 2022 |access-date=18 October 2024}}</ref>

In 2021, [[China]] announced a law which forbade minors from playing video games{{snd}}which they described as "spiritual opium" – for more than three hours a week.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Goh|first=Brenda|date=31 August 2021|title=Three hours a week: Play time's over for China's young video gamers|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/china/china-rolls-out-new-rules-minors-online-gaming-xinhua-2021-08-30/|access-date=28 December 2021}}</ref> With China being a large market, the law raised concerns about the future of esports within the country.<ref>{{Cite web|last1=Klein|first1=Frankfurt Kurnit|last2=Jensen|first2=Selz PC-Frances|date=4 October 2021|title=The Chinese Government Bans PUBG Esports Among Stricter Regulations for Video Games|url=https://www.lexology.com/library/detail.aspx?g=6cfe5fb8-472c-44d7-b28d-f94bb9960ff0|access-date=28 December 2021|website=Lexology|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Standaert|first=Michael|title=Will teen gaming clampdown deal a knockout to China's esports?|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2021/9/10/will-teen-gaming-clampdown-deal-china-esports-a-technical-ko|access-date=28 December 2021|website=www.aljazeera.com|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=9 September 2021|title=Chinese Esports Powerhouses Struggle as New Gaming Hours Ban Hits|url=https://www.esportsgrizzly.com/industry/chinese-esports-powerhouses-struggle-as-new-gaming-hours-ban-hits/|access-date=28 December 2021|website=Esports Grizzly|language=en-US|archive-date=14 March 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230314074543/https://www.esportsgrizzly.com/industry/chinese-esports-powerhouses-struggle-as-new-gaming-hours-ban-hits/|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Classification as a sport==
[[File:2019 SEA Games Esports Tekken 7 THA vs PHI 2.jpg|thumb|A match of ''[[Tekken 7]]'' at the [[Esports at the 2019 Southeast Asian Games|2019 Southeast Asian Games]]. Esports was a medal event at the regional games which featured mostly traditional sports.]]
Labeling competitive video games as a [[sport]] is a controversial topic.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://johancruyffinstitute.com/en/blog-en/esports-sport-or-business/ |title=eSports, sport or business? |website=Johan Cruyff Institute|date=27 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170918211929/https://johancruyffinstitute.com/en/blog-en/esports-sport-or-business/|archive-date=18 September 2017}}</ref><ref>Ivo v. Hilvoorde & Niek Pot (2016) [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/301774466_Embodiment_and_fundamental_motor_skills_in_eSports Embodiment and fundamental motor skills in eSports], Sport, Ethics and Philosophy, 10:1, 14–27, {{doi|10.1080/17511321.2016.1159246}}</ref><ref>Ivo van Hilvoorde (2016) [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/303016888_Hilvoorde_I_van_2016_Sport_and_play_in_a_digital_world_guest_editorial_Sport_Ethics_and_Philosophy_DOI_1010801751132120161171252 Sport and play in a digital world], Sport, Ethics and Philosophy, 10:1, 1–4, {{doi|10.1080/17511321.2016.1171252}}</ref> Proponents<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tjønndal|first=Anne|date=23 September 2020|title="What's next? Calling beer-drinking a sport?!": virtual resistance to considering eSport as sport|url=https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/SBM-10-2019-0085/full/html|journal=Sport, Business and Management|language=en|volume=11|issue=1|pages=72–88|doi=10.1108/SBM-10-2019-0085|s2cid=224973999|issn=2042-678X|url-access=subscription}}</ref> argue that esports are a fast-growing "non-traditional sport" which requires "careful planning, precise timing, and skillful execution".<ref>{{cite web|author=Tom Burns|date=26 July 2014|title='E-Sports' can now drop the 'e'|url=http://www.aljazeera.com/indepth/opinion/2014/07/esports-can-now-drop-e-2014724112549724248.html|access-date=20 September 2015|publisher=Al Jazeera}}</ref> Others claim that sports involve physical fitness and physical training, and prefer to classify esports as a [[mind sport]].<ref>{{cite web|title=E-Sports and Other Games|url=http://www.worldmindsportsfederation.com/mind-sports/e-sports-and-other-games.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151208045001/http://www.worldmindsportsfederation.com/mind-sports/e-sports-and-other-games.aspx|archive-date=8 December 2015|access-date=23 August 2015|publisher=World Mind Sports Federation}}</ref>

Former [[ESPN]] president [[John Skipper]] described esports in 2014 as a competition and "not a sport".<ref>{{cite news |url=http://ftw.usatoday.com/2014/09/espn-esports-league-of-legends-dota |title=ESPN's president says that eSports are not 'real sports,' and he's wrong |newspaper=[[USA Today]] |last=Schwartz |first=Nick |date=6 September 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.vg247.com/2014/09/08/espn-boss-says-esports-are-not-real-sports/ |title=ESPN boss says eSports are not "real sports" |website=[[VG247]] |last=Hillier |first=Brenna |date=8 September 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.engadget.com/2014/09/08/espn-boss-e-sports-arent-sports/ |title=ESPN boss: E-sports aren't sports |publisher=[[Engadget]] |last=Reahard |first=Jef |date=8 September 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/insertcoin/2014/09/07/espn-boss-declares-esports-not-a-sport/ |title=ESPN Boss Declares eSports 'Not A Sport' |magazine=[[Forbes]] |last=Tassi |first=Paul |date=7 September 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.polygon.com/2014/10/1/6864047/esports-espn-league-of-legends-lol-starcraft |title=Does eSports need ESPN before the mainstream accepts it? |website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] |last=Gera |first=Emily |date=1 October 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/espn-says-esports-isnt-a-sport-what-do-you-think/1100-6422148/ |title=ESPN Says eSports Isn't a Sport – What Do You Think? |website=GameSpot |author=Emanuel Maiberg |date=6 September 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref> In 2013 on an episode of [[Real Sports with Bryant Gumbel]] the panelist openly laughed at the topic.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sarkar |first1=Samit |title=HBO's 'Real Sports' debates the merits of eSports |url=http://www.polygon.com/2013/12/18/5225226/hbo-real-sports-debate-is-esports-a-sport |website=Polygon |date=18 December 2013 |access-date=13 May 2015}}</ref> In addition, many in the fighting games community maintain a distinction between their competitive gaming competitions and the more commercially connected esports competitions of other genres.<ref name="momentumMatters">{{cite web |last=Graham |first=David Philip |title=Guest Editorial – Momentum Matters: A Historical Perspective on the FGC and eSports |url=http://shoryuken.com/2011/12/12/guest-editorial-momentum-matters-a-historical-perspective-on-the-fgc-and-esports-communities-2/ |publisher=Shoryuken.com |date=12 December 2011 |access-date=6 June 2012 |archive-date=2 August 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170802073526/http://shoryuken.com/2011/12/12/guest-editorial-momentum-matters-a-historical-perspective-on-the-fgc-and-esports-communities-2/ }}</ref> In the 2015 World Championship hosted by the [[International Esports Federation]], an esports panel of guests from international sports society discussed the future recognition of esports as a legitimate sport.<ref>{{cite AV media |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QTEk0bh0GUQ |title=[2015 IESF] e-Sports Summit with International Sports Society -EsportsTV |date=3 December 2015 |via=YouTube}}</ref>

Russia was the first country that classified "cybersport" as an official sport discipline<ref>{{Cite news|title=Как Россия первой в мире признала киберспорт|url=https://matchtv.ru/cyber/matchtvnews_NI678327_Kak_Rossija_pervoj_v_mire_priznala_kibersport|access-date=23 October 2017|language=ru}}</ref> on 25 July 2001.<ref name=komsport2001>Приказ Госкомспорта РФ от 25 July 2001 № 449 «О введении видов спорта в государственные программы физического воспитания»</ref> After a series of reforms in Russian sports, it was classified as a sport again on 12 March 2004.<ref name=komsport2001 /><ref>Утв. приказом Госкомспорта РФ от 14 April 2003 № 225 «О перечне видов спорта, признанных федеральным органом исполнительной власти в области физической культуры и спорта» с последующими изменениями.</ref><ref name=fedagent2006>Приказ Федерального агентства по физической культуре и спорту от 4 июля 2006 г № 414 «О компьютерном спорте»</ref><ref>Положение «О Всероссийском реестре видов спорта (ВРВС)» (утв. Приказом Федерального агентства по физической культуре, спорту и туризму от 28 сентября 2004 г № 273)</ref> In July 2006, it was removed from a list of sport disciplines because it did not fit the new sport standards.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.proplay.ru/news/2030/|title=ProPlay / Новости / Киберспорт более не имеет официального статуса|website=www.proplay.ru}}</ref><ref>См. Приказ Федерального агентства по физической культуре и спорту от 4 июля 2006 г № 414 «О компьютерном спорте»; Положение «О Всероссийском реестре видов спорта (ВРВС)» (утв. Приказом Федерального агентства по физической культуре, спорту и туризму от 28 сентября 2004 г № 273).</ref> On 7 July 2016, [[Ministry of Sport (Russia)|The Ministry of Sport]] decided to add cybersport into the sport registry<ref name="pravo-esports">{{cite web|url=http://publication.pravo.gov.ru/Document/View/0001201606070022?index=0&rangeSize=1|title=Официальный интернет-портал правовой информации|publisher=publication.pravo.gov.ru|access-date=8 June 2016|archive-date=11 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160611013229/http://publication.pravo.gov.ru/Document/View/0001201606070022?index=0&rangeSize=1}}</ref> and on 13 April 2017, esports become an official sport discipline once again.{{Citation needed|date=October 2021}}

China was another one of the first countries to recognize esports as a real sport in 2003,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lu |first=Zhouxiang |date=11 December 2016 |title=From E-Heroin to E-Sports: The Development of Competitive Gaming in China |journal=The International Journal of the History of Sport |volume=33 |issue=18 |pages=2186–2206 |doi=10.1080/09523367.2017.1358167 |s2cid=148906225 |issn=0952-3367}}</ref> despite concerns at the time that video games were addictive. Through this, the government encouraged esports, stating that by participating in esports, players were also "training the body for China".<ref>{{cite journal | title = Game On: The Rise of the eSports Middle Kingdom | first = Haiqing | last = Yu | date = 2018 | journal = Media Industries| volume = 5 | issue = 1 | doi = 10.3998/mij.15031809.0005.106 | doi-access = free | hdl = 2027/spo.15031809.0005.106 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> Furthermore, by early 2019, China recognized esports players as an official profession within the [[Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security]]'s Occupation Skill Testing Authority recommendations, as well as professional gaming operators, those that distribute and manage esports games.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://variety.com/2019/gaming/news/osta-china-gaming-profession-1203126468/ | title = China to Recognize Gaming as Official Profession | first = Emily | last= Gera | date = 1 February 2019 | access-date = 24 September 2019 | work = [[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] }}</ref> By July 2019, more than 100,000 people had registered themselves as professional gamers under this, with the Ministry stating that they anticipate over 2 million such people in this profession in five years.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2019-07-19/beijing-pushing-esports-could-cause-culture-clashes | title = Chinese governments hand out cash, subsidies to encourage esports development | first = Shuli | last= Ren | date = 19 July 2019 | work = [[Bloomberg L.P.]] | via =[[Los Angeles Times]] }}</ref>

In 2013, Canadian ''League of Legends'' player [[Shiphtur|Danny "Shiphtur" Le]] became the first pro gamer to receive an American [[P-1A visa]], a category designated for "Internationally Recognized Athletes".<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-online-gamers-20130808-story.html |title=Online game League of Legends star gets U.S. visa as pro athlete |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |author=Paresh Dave |date=7 August 2013 |access-date=4 December 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.uscis.gov/portal/site/uscis/menuitem.eb1d4c2a3e5b9ac89243c6a7543f6d1a/?vgnextchannel=19860b89284a3210VgnVCM100000b92ca60aRCRD&vgnextoid=19860b89284a3210VgnVCM100000b92ca60aRCRD |title=P-1A Internationally Recognized Athlete |publisher=US Citizenship and Immigration Services |access-date=7 October 2013}}</ref> In 2014, Turkey's [[Ministry of Youth and Sports (Turkey)|Ministry of Youth and Sports]] started issuing esports licenses to players certified as professionals.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.merlininkazani.com/sizler-de-lisansli-e-sporcu-olabilirsiniz-espor-70805|title=Sizler de lisanslı E-Sporcu olabilirsiniz |work=Oyun Haberleri - merlininkazani.com |date=8 February 2014 |access-date=17 January 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://5mid.com/espor-nedir |title=E-Spor Nedir? |access-date=17 January 2018 |archive-date=29 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180129031327/http://5mid.com/espor-nedir }}</ref> In 2016, the French government started working on a project to regulate and recognize esports.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://venturebeat.com/2016/05/03/french-government-announces-plans-to-legalize-and-regulate-esports-industry/ |title=French government announces plans to legalize and regulate esports industry |website=VentureBeat |date=3 May 2016 |access-date=14 September 2016 |archive-date=23 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171023012221/https://venturebeat.com/2016/05/03/french-government-announces-plans-to-legalize-and-regulate-esports-industry/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> The [[Games and Amusements Board]] of the Philippines started issuing athletic licenses to Filipino esports players who are vouched for by a professional esports team in July 2017.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sheldon |first1=David |title=Philippines Officially Recognizes eSports As A Real Sport |url=https://www.casino.org/blog/philippines-officially-recognizes-esports-as-a-real-sport/ |access-date=22 October 2017 |work=Casino Org |date=22 October 2017}}</ref><ref name="abs-cbn">{{cite news |last1=Regalado |first1=Pia |title=The Philippines' new athletes: eSports gamers |url=https://www.abs-cbn.com/focus/10/10/17/the-philippines-new-athletes-esports-gamers |access-date=22 October 2017 |publisher=ABS-CBN |date=10 October 2017}}</ref>

To help promote esports as a legitimate sport, several esports events have been run alongside more traditional international sports competitions. The [[2007 Asian Indoor Games]] was the first notable multi-sport competition including esports as an official medal-winning event, alongside other traditional sports, and the later editions of the [[Asian Indoor Games]], as well as its successor the [[Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games]], have always included esports as an official medal event or an exhibition event up to now. Moreover, the [[Asian Games]], which is the Asian top-level multi-sport competition, also included esports as a medal event at the [[2022 Asian Games|2022 edition]]; esports around games such as ''Hearthstone'', ''Starcraft II'', and ''League of Legends'' were [[Esports at the 2018 Asian Games|presented as an exhibition event]] at the [[2018 Asian Games]] as a lead-in to the 2022 games.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://compete.kotaku.com/esports-will-become-a-medal-event-at-the-2022-asian-gam-1794431163 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170419104106/http://compete.kotaku.com/esports-will-become-a-medal-event-at-the-2022-asian-gam-1794431163 |archive-date=19 April 2017 |title=Esports Will Become A Medal Event At The 2022 Asian Games |first=Maddy |last=Myers |date=18 April 2017 |access-date=18 April 2017 |work=[[Kotaku]]}}</ref><ref name="ap 2018 asian games"/> The [[2019 Southeast Asian Games]] included six medal events for esports.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamer.com/esports-is-an-official-medal-event-at-the-southeast-asian-games/ | title = Esports is an official medal event at the Southeast Asian Games |first = Fraser | last =Brown | date = 28 November 2018 | access-date = 28 November 2018 | work = [[PC Gamer]] }}</ref> Since 2018, [[World Sailing]] has held an [[eSailing World Championship]] that showed a main sports federation embracing esports.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sailing.org/news/89460.php|title=Velista71 wins eSailing World Championship title|website=sailing.org}}</ref> The [[Virtual Regatta]] race shadowing the [[2020-2021 Vendee Globe]] was the first online game believe to have in excess of 1,000,000 unique users<ref>{{cite web|url=https://blogs.sw.siemens.com/simcenter/vendee-globe-a-digital-twist/|title = Vendée Globe: A digital twist?|date = 4 February 2021}}</ref>

Ahead of [[The International 2021]], which was originally set to take place in [[Stockholm]] in 2020, the [[Swedish Sports Confederation]] voted in June 2021 to deny recognition of esports as a sporting event, which jeopardized plans for how Valve had arranged the event in regards to travel visas for international players. Valve had tried to work with Sweden to accommodate players, but eventually rescheduled the event to Romania instead.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.theverge.com/2021/6/22/22545319/dota-2-the-international-valve-sweden-europe | title = Dota 2's The International might not take place in Sweden after all | first = Jay | last = Peters | date = 22 June 2021 | access-date = 22 June 2021 | work = [[The Verge]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamesn.com/dota-2/ti10-date-romania | title = Dota 2's The International gets new dates after Sweden says no to esports | first = Dustin | last = Bailey | date = 7 July 2021 | access-date = 8 July 2021 | work = [[PCGamesN]] }}</ref>

The [[2022 Commonwealth Games]] featured esports competitions as a pilot ahead of being a potential full medal event for 2026.<ref>{{cite web | url  =https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2022-02-09-esports-coming-to-the-2022-commonwealth-games | title = Esports coming to 2022 Commonwealth Games | first =  Victoria | last = Kennedy | date = 9 February 2022 | access-date = 9 February 2022 | work = [[Eurogamer]] }}</ref>

In [[Greece]], in March 2022 a law entered into force recognising and regulating esports<ref>[https://www.e-nomothesia.gr/kat-athlitismos/nomos-4908-2022-phek-52a-11-3-2022.html Law 4908/2022], articles 28–35, published and entered into force on 11 March 2022.</ref> and in June 2023, the relevant federation for esports has been officially given recognition<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ανάρτηση Πράξεων στο Διαδίκτυο {{!}} Πρόγραμμα Δι@ύγεια – Απόφαση χορήγησης ειδικής αθλητικής αναγνώρισης στην "ΕΛΛΗΝΙΚΗ ΟΜΟΣΠΟΝΔΙΑ ΗΛΕΚΤΡΟΝΙΚΟΥ ΑΘΛΗΤΙΣΜΟΥ" για τα ηλεκτρονικά αθλήματα (e-sports). |url=https://diavgeia.gov.gr/decision/view/9%CE%9B%CE%A754653%CE%A04-%CE%A72%CE%91 |access-date=15 June 2023 |website=diavgeia.gov.gr}}</ref> and included in the list of sports federations.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ΟΜΟΣΠΟΝΔΙΕΣ |url=https://gga.gov.gr/epopteyomenoi-foreis/omospondies |access-date=15 June 2023 |website=gga.gov.gr |date=14 November 2012 }}</ref>

===Olympic Games recognition===
The [[Olympic Games]] are also seen as a potential method to legitimize esports. A summit held by the [[International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) in October 2017 acknowledged the growing popularity of esports, concluding that "Competitive 'esports' could be considered as a sporting activity, and the players involved prepare and train with an intensity which may be comparable to athletes in traditional sports" but would require any games used for the Olympics fitting "with the rules and regulations of the Olympic movement".<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.businessinsider.com/e-sports-gets-closer-to-being-part-of-the-olympics-games-2017-10 |title=E-sports just got closer to being part of the Olympics |first=Karolos |last=Grohmann |date=28 October 2017 |access-date=5 November 2017 |agency=[[Reuters]]}}</ref> Another article by Andy Stout suggests that 106 million people viewed the [[2017 League of Legends World Championship|2017 Worlds Esports competition]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Andy Stout2017-11-10T11:51:00+00:00 |title=How big is the eSports opportunity? |url=https://www.ibc.org/trends/how-big-is-the-esports-opportunity/2533.article |access-date=9 November 2022 |website=IBC |language=en}}</ref> International Olympic Committee (IOC) president [[Thomas Bach]] has noted that the IOC is troubled by violent games and the lack of a global sanctioning body for esports.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.polygon.com/2017/8/30/16228134/olympics-esports-violent-video-games |title=If esports come to the Olympics, don't expect to see 'violent' titles |first=Owen |last=Good |date=30 August 2017 |access-date=30 August 2017 |work=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]}}</ref><ref name="ap 2018 asian games">{{cite web | url = https://apnews.com/3615bd17ebb8478ab534691080a9a32a | title = Bach: No Olympic future for esports until 'violence' removed | first = Stephen | last = Wade | date = 1 September 2018 | access-date = 3 September 2018 | publisher = [[Associated Press]] }}</ref> Bach acknowledged that many Olympic sports originated from violent combat, but stated that "sport is the civilized expression about this. If you have egames where it's about killing somebody, this cannot be brought into line with our Olympic values."<ref name="ap 2018 asian games"/> Due to that, the IOC suggested that they would approve more esports centered around games that simulate real sports, such as the ''[[NBA 2K]]'' or ''[[FIFA (video game series)|FIFA]]'' series.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://arstechnica.com/gaming/2018/03/olympic-committee-open-to-esports-but-only-without-violence/ | title = Violent video games not welcome for Olympic esports consideration | first = Kyle | last = Orland | date = 13 March 2018 | access-date = 14 March 2018 | work = [[Ars Technica]] }}</ref>

The issues around esports have not prevented the IOC from exploring what possibilities there are for incorporation into future Olympics. In July 2018, the IOC and the [[Global Association of International Sports Federations]] (GAISF) held a symposium and invited major figures in esports, including [[Epic Games]]' [[Mark Rein (software executive)|Mark Rein]], [[Blizzard Entertainment]]'s [[Mike Morhaime]], and esports players Dario "TLO" Wünsch, [[Jake (video game player)|Jacob "Jake" Lyon]], and [[Geguri|Se-yeon "Geguri" Kim]], for these organizations "to gain a deeper understanding of esports, their impact and likely future development, so that [they] can jointly consider the ways in which [they] may collaborate to the mutual benefit of all of sport in the years ahead".<ref>{{cite web | url = https://globalnews.ca/news/4340744/esports-in-olympics/ | title = Video gaming as an Olympic sport? IOC hosting eSports forum to better understand competitive gaming | first= Adam | last = Frisk | date = 19 July 2018 | access-date = 20 July 2018 | work = [[Global News]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.ign.com/articles/2018/07/20/overwatch-players-involved-in-talks-with-olympic-committee-to-discuss-esports-opportunities | title = Overwatch Players Involved In Talks With Olympic Committee To Discuss Esports Opportunities | first = Michael | last= Dominaco | date = 20 July 2018 | access-date = 20 July 2018 | work = [[IGN]] }}</ref> The IOC has tested the potential for esports through exhibition games. With support from the IOC, [[Intel]] sponsored exhibition esports events for ''[[StarCraft II]]'' and ''[[Steep (video game)|Steep]]'' prior to the [[2018 Winter Olympics]] in [[Pyeongchang]], and five South Korean esports players were part of the [[Olympic Torch]] relay.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://olympics.nbcsports.com/2017/11/03/esports-pyeongchang-olympics-extreme-masters/ |title=Esports event in PyeongChang before Olympics supported by IOC |first=Nick |last=Zaccardi |date=3 November 2017 |access-date=5 November 2017 |work=[[NBC News]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine | url = https://www.wired.com/story/esports-pyeongchang-olympics/ | title = ESPORTS ZERG-RUSH THE OLYMPICS—BUT CAN THEY BECOME OFFICIAL EVENTS? | first= Phuc | last =Pham | date = 9 February 2018 | access-date =10 February 2018 | magazine = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] }}</ref> A similar exhibition showcase, the [[eGames (esports)|eGames]], was held alongside the [[2016 Summer Olympics]] in [[Rio de Janeiro]], though this was not supported by the IOC.

During the Eighth Olympic Summit in December 2019, the IOC reiterated that it would only consider sports-simulating games for any official Olympic event, but it would look at two paths for such games in the future: those that promoted good physical and mental health lifestyles, and [[virtual reality]] and [[augmented reality]] games that included physical activity.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.sportbusiness.com/news/ioc-to-form-two-speed-esports-strategy/ | title = IOC to form 'two-speed' esports strategy | date = 9 December 2019 | access-date = 10 December 2019 | work = [[Sports Business]] }}</ref>

In the late 2010s, leaders in Japan became involved in helping bring esports to the [[2020 Summer Olympics]] and beyond, given the country's reputation as a major video game industry centre. Esports in Japan had not flourished due to the country's anti-gambling laws that also prevent paid professional gaming tournaments, but there were efforts starting in late 2017 to eliminate this issue.<ref name="bloomberg olympics 2024"/> At the suggestion of the [[Tokyo Organising Committee of the Olympic and Paralympic Games|Tokyo Olympic Games Committee]] for the 2020 Summer Olympics, four esports organizations have worked with Japan's leading [[consumer organization]] to exempt esports tournaments from gambling law restrictions. [[Takeo Kawamura (politician)|Takeo Kawamura]], a member of the [[House of Representatives (Japan)|Japanese House of Representatives]] and of the ruling [[Liberal Democratic Party (Japan)|Liberal Democratic Party]], led a coalition of ruling and opposing politicians to support esports, called the Japan esports Union, or JeSU.<ref name="bloomberg japan jul2018">{{cite news | url = https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-07-10/this-139-year-old-company-has-a-plan-to-get-millennials-excited | title = You Can Now Officially Play Esports for Money in Japan | first1 = Yuri | last1 = Nakamura | first2= Yuki | last2= Furikawa | date =10 July 2018 | access-date = 13 July 2018 | work = [[Bloomberg L.P.]] }}</ref> Kawamura said that they would be willing to pass laws to further exempt esports as needed so that esports athletes can make a living playing these sports. So far, this has resulted in the ability of esports players to obtain exemption licenses to allow them to play, a similar mechanism needed for professional athletes in other sports in Japan to play professionally.<ref name="bloomberg olympics 2024">{{cite news | url = https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-01-18/shinzo-abe-s-party-wants-japan-ready-for-video-games-in-olympics | title = Shinzo Abe's Party Wants Japan Ready for Video Games in Olympics |author1=Yuji Nakamura |author2=Emi Nobuhiro |author3=Takako Taniguchi | date = 18 January 2018 | access-date = 19 January 2018 | work = [[Bloomberg Businessweek]] }}</ref> The first such licenses were given out in mid-July 2018, via a tournament held by several video game publishers to award prizes to many players but with JeSU offering these exemption licenses to the top dozen or so players that emerge, allowing them to compete in further esports events.<ref name="bloomberg japan jul2018"/> The Tokyo Olympic Committee has also planned to arrange a number of esports events leading up to the 2020 games.<ref name="bloomberg olympics 2024"/> With the IOC, five esports events were set as part of an Olympic Virtual Series from 13 May to 23 June 2021, ahead of the games. Each event in auto racing, baseball, cycling, rowing and sailing will be managed by an IOC-recognized governing body for the sport along with a video game publisher of a game for that sport. For example, the auto racing event will be based on the ''[[GT racing|Gran Turismo]]'' series and overseen by the [[International Automobile Federation]] along with [[Polyphony Digital]]. The baseball, cycling, and [[ESailing World Championship#Olympics Virtual Series (OVS) Esailing Champions|esailing]] events will be based on ''[[Power Pros|eBaseball Powerful Pro Baseball 2020]]'', ''[[Zwift]]'', and ''[[Virtual Regatta]]'', respectively.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/esports/2021/04/22/ioc-olympics-esports/ | title = IOC announces inaugural slate of Olympic-licensed esports events | first = Des | last = Bieler | date = 22 April 2021 | access-date = 23 April 2021 | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] }}</ref>

The organization committee for the [[2024 Summer Olympics]] in Paris were in discussions with the IOC and the various professional esports organizations to consider esports for the event, citing the need to include these elements to keep the Olympics relevant to younger generations.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.espn.co.uk/olympics/story/_/id/20286757/paris-open-esports-competition-2024-summer-olympics |title=Paris Olympic bid committee is open to esports on 2024 Olympic program |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=9 August 2017 |access-date=9 August 2017}}</ref> Ultimately, the organization committee determined esports were premature to bring to the 2024 Games as medal events, but have not ruled out other activities related to esports during the Games.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://fortune.com/2018/12/10/olympics-video-games-paris-2024/ | title = Video Games Won't Be Part of the Paris Olympics | first= Chris | last= Morris | date = 10 December 2018 | access-date = 10 December 2018 | work = [[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]] }}</ref>

In September 2021, the Olympic Council of Asia announced eight esports games will officially debut as medal sports for the 2022 Asian Games in Hangzhou, China.<ref>{{cite web|last=Daniels|first=Tom|date=8 September 2021|title=LoL, Dota 2, and Street Fighter V among 2022 Asian Games medal events|url=https://esportsinsider.com/2021/09/lol-dota-2-and-street-fighter-v-among-2022-asian-games-medal-events/|access-date=15 November 2021|website=Esports Insider|language=en-GB}}</ref>

In December 2021, the IOC confirmed its Olympic Virtual Series (OVS) will return in 2022. The first edition of the OVS which ran from 13 May to 23 June, featured nearly 250,000 participants and had more than two million entries.<ref>{{cite web|date=13 December 2021|title=IOC's Olympic Virtual Series to return in 2022|url=https://www.sportspromedia.com/news/ioc-olympic-virtual-series-2022-esports-gaming/|work =Sports Pro|language=en-GB}}</ref>

In January 2022, the IOC announced the appointment of the organization's first ever head of virtual sport, tasked with the development of virtual sport for the global Olympic body, increasing the organization's engagement with gaming communities, and overseeing the Olympic Virtual Series, IOC's first licensed non-physical sports event. The inaugural series included virtual baseball, cycling, rowing, [[Esailing World Championship#Olympics Virtual Series (OVS) Esailing Champions|esailing]] and motorsports events.<ref>{{cite web|date=17 January 2022|title=IOC hires Vincent Pereira as first ever head of virtual sport|url=https://www.sportspromedia.com/news/ioc-vincent-pereira-virtual-sport-head-esports-olympics/|work =Sports Pro|language=en-GB}}</ref>

In February 2022, the [[Commonwealth Games Federation]] announced that esports would be included in the [[2022 Commonwealth Games]] as a pilot event, with the possibility of it being a medal event in the [[2026 Commonwealth Games|2026 Games]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Esports to be included as pilot event at 2022 Commonwealth Games |url=https://www.espn.com/olympics/story/_/id/33252463/esports-included-pilot-event-2022-commonwealth-games |access-date=17 April 2022 |work=[[ESPN]] |agency=[[Reuters]] |date=9 February 2022}}</ref> The inaugural Commonwealth Esports Championship had separate branding, medals, and organization and included both men and women's ''[[Dota 2]]'', ''[[Pro Evolution Soccer|eFootball]]'', and ''[[Rocket League]]'' events.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Freeman |first1=Jay |title=Esports: Commonwealth Games trial an 'opportunity to show it is more than just a game' |url=https://www.bbc.com/sport/commonwealth-games/60632666 |access-date=17 April 2022 |work=[[BBC]] |date=22 March 2022}}</ref>

As a follow-up to 2021's Olympic Virtual Series, the IOC and the [[Singapore National Olympic Council]] held an [[Olympic Esports Week]] in Singapore in June 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Olympic Esports Series will feature 'Just Dance,' 'Gran Turismo' and chess |url=https://www.engadget.com/the-olympic-esports-series-will-feature-just-dance-gran-turismo-and-chess-172704742.html |access-date=2 March 2023 |website=Engadget |date=March 2023 |language=en-US}}</ref> Games featured at the event included ''Tic Tac Bow'' (archery), ''[[Power Pros|WBSC eBaseball: Power Pros]]'' (baseball), [[Chess.com]] (chess), ''[[Zwift]]'' (cycling), ''[[Just Dance (video game series)|Just Dance]]'' (dancing), ''[[Gran Turismo (series)|Gran Turismo]]'' (motorsport), ''[[Virtual Regatta]]'' ([[Esailing World Championship#Olympics Virtual Series (OVS) Esailing Champions|esailing]]), ''[[Fortnite]]'' (sharpshooting), ''Virtual Taekwondo'' (taekwondo), and ''Tennis Clash'' (tennis).<ref>{{cite press release | url = https://olympics.com/ioc/news/ioc-announces-olympic-esports-series-2023 | title = IOC announces Olympic Esports Series 2023 with winners to be crowned at live finals in Singapore from 22 to 25 June | publisher = [[International Olympic Committee]] | date = 1 March 2023 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.engadget.com/fortnite-is-now-an-olympic-esport-143312772.html |  title = The Olympic Esports Series will feature 'Just Dance,' 'Gran Turismo' and chess | first = Jon | last = Fingas | date = 5 May 2023 | access-date = 5 May 2023 | work = [[Engadget]] }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=5 May 2023 |title=Ticket details released for first-ever Olympic Esports Week, with sport shooting joining the competition line-up |url=https://olympics.com/ioc/news/ticket-details-released-for-first-ever-olympic-esports-week |access-date=3 November 2023 |website=International Olympic Committee}}</ref>

==Games==
{{main|List of esports games}}

A number of games are popular among professional competitors. The tournaments which emerged in the mid-1990s coincided with the popularity of [[fighting game]]s and [[first-person shooter]]s, genres which still maintain a devoted fan base. In the 2000s, [[real-time strategy]] games became overwhelmingly popular in South Korean [[internet café]]s, with crucial influence on the development of esports worldwide. Competitions exist for many titles and genres, though the most popular games{{Citation needed|date=December 2021}} as of the early 2020s are ''[[Counter-Strike: Global Offensive]]'', ''[[Call of Duty]]'', ''[[League of Legends]]'', ''[[Dota 2]]'', ''[[Fortnite Battle Royale|Fortnite]]'', ''[[Rocket League]]'', ''[[Valorant]]'', ''[[Hearthstone (video game)|Hearthstone]]'', ''[[Super Smash Bros. Melee]]'', ''[[StarCraft II]]'' and ''[[Overwatch (video game)|Overwatch]]''.<ref name="momentum">{{cite web |url=http://www.pcgamesn.com/starcraft/2012-esports-battle-momentum-between-league-legends-starcraft-2-and-dota-2 |title=2012 in eSports: the battle for momentum between League of Legends, StarCraft 2, and Dota 2 |publisher=PC Games N |author=robzacny |date=31 December 2012 |access-date=15 November 2013}}</ref> ''[[Hearthstone: Heroes of Warcraft|Hearthstone]]'' has also popularized the [[digital collectible card game]] (DCCG) genre since its release in 2014.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Clark |first1=Tim |title=What I learned from playing with a professional Hearthstone coach |url=http://www.pcgamer.com/hearthstone-help-what-i-learned-from-playing-with-a-professional-coach/ |website=www.pcgamer.com |date=20 August 2014 |access-date=22 February 2015}}</ref>

==Video game design==
{{see also|Video game design}}

While it is common for video games to be designed with the experience of the player in game being the only priority, many successful esports games have been designed to be played professionally from the beginning. Developers may decide to add dedicated esports features, or even make design compromises to support high level competition. Games such as ''StarCraft II'',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://kotaku.com/the-sacrifices-of-starcraft-ii-made-in-the-name-of-spor-5777029 |title=The Sacrifices of StarCraft II Made In The Name of Sports |publisher=Kotaku |author=Michael McWhertor |date=4 March 2011 |access-date=8 October 2013}}</ref> ''League of Legends'',<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pcgamesn.com/leagueoflegends/how-riot-games-are-building-better-league-legends-and-catching-their-own-success |title=How Riot Games are building a better League of Legends, and catching up to their own success |publisher=PC GamesN |author=robzacny |date=24 October 2012 |access-date=8 October 2013}}</ref> and ''Dota 2''<ref>{{cite web |url=http://esportsbusiness.com/valve-show-developers-how-to-support-esports-with-dota-2/ |title=Valve show developers how to support eSports with Dota 2 |author=Alan LaFleur |work=eSports Business |date=21 June 2012 |access-date=8 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131222120743/http://esportsbusiness.com/valve-show-developers-how-to-support-esports-with-dota-2/ |archive-date=22 December 2013 }}</ref> have all been designed, at least in part, to support professional competition.
