For example, the organization [[Misfits Gaming]] has hired a psychologist to ensure players are equipped with methods to deal with stress and anxiety.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stubbs |first=Mike |title=Why Esports Team Misfits Is Prioritizing Mental Health For Players And Staff |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/mikestubbs/2021/06/09/why-esports-team-misfits-is-prioritizing-mental-health-for-players-and-staff/ |access-date=15 February 2023 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref>

===Ethical issues===
Esports athletes are usually obligated to behave ethically, abiding by both the explicit rules set out by tournaments, associations, and teams, as well as following general expectations of good [[sportsmanship]]. For example, it is common practice and considered good etiquette to send a "gg" (good game) message to opponents when defeated.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.techhive.com/article/248526/web_jargon_origins_revealed.html |title=Web Jargon Origins Revealed |author=David Daw |work=TechHive |date=21 January 2012 |access-date=22 September 2013 |archive-date=15 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151015235725/http://www.techhive.com/article/248526/web_jargon_origins_revealed.html }}</ref> Many games rely on competitors having limited information about the game state. In a prominent example of good conduct, during a 2012 [[Intel Extreme Masters|IEM]] ''StarCraft II'' game, players Feast and DeMusliM voluntarily offered information about their strategies to negate the influence of outside information inadvertently leaked to Feast during the game.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cadred.org/News/Article/167534/ |title=IEM Sao Paolo: Manner Bear Conflict |publisher=Cadred |author=Victor Meulendijks |date=8 February 2012 |access-date=8 October 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20131008224558/http://www.cadred.org/News/Article/167534/ |archive-date=8 October 2013 }}</ref> Players in some leagues have been reprimanded for failing to meet expectations of good behavior. In 2012, professional ''League of Legends'' player Christian "IWillDominate" Riviera was banned from competing for one year following a history of verbal abuse.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://forums.na.leagueoflegends.com/board/showthread.php?t=2864421 |title=IWillDominate Tribunal Permaban & eSports Competition Ruling |date=4 December 2012 |access-date=9 November 2014 |archive-date=26 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171026045406/http://forums.na.leagueoflegends.com/board/showthread.php?t=2864421 }}</ref> In 2013, ''StarCraft II'' progamer [[Greg "Idra" Fields]] was fired from [[Evil Geniuses]] for insulting his fans on the [[Team Liquid]] internet forums.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.teamliquid.net/forum/viewmessage.php?topic_id=411840 |title=Evil Geniuses Releases Greg "IdrA" Fields |author=Alexander Garfield |publisher=TeamLiquid |date=10 May 2013 |access-date=8 January 2014}}</ref> ''League of Legends'' players Mithy and Nukeduck received similar penalties in 2014 after behaving in a "toxic" manner during matches.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/league-of-legends-pro-players-banned-for-toxic-behavior/1100-6420072/ |title=League of Legends Pro Players Banned for "Toxic Behavior" |date=3 June 2014 |access-date=22 February 2015}}</ref>

There have been serious rule violations in certain esports. In 2010, eleven ''StarCraft: Brood War'' players were found guilty of [[StarCraft professional competition#Match fixing scandal|fixing matches for profit]] and were fined and banned from future competition. [[Team Curse]] and [[Team Dignitas]] were denied prize money for collusion during the [[2012 MLG Summer Championship]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pcgamesn.com/leagueoflegends/league-legends-curse-na-and-team-dignitas-disqualified-mlg-summer-championship-no-first-or-second-place-awarded |title=League of Legends' Curse NA and Team Dignitas disqualified from MLG Summer Championship, no first or second place awarded |author=Jeremy Peel |publisher=PC GamesN |date=27 August 2012 |access-date=22 September 2013}}</ref> In 2012, ''League of Legends'' team Azubu Frost was fined US$30,000 for cheating during a semifinal match of the world playoffs.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/news/riot-fines-league-of-legends-cheaters-30000-6398055 |title=Riot fines League of Legends cheaters $30,000 |author=Laura Parker |website=GameSpot |date=10 October 2012 |access-date=22 September 2013}}</ref> ''Dota 2'' player Aleksey "Solo" Berezin was suspended from several tournaments for intentionally throwing a game to collect $322 from online gambling.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.joindota.com/en/news/10165-solo-out-of-rox-kis |title=Solo out of Rox.KIS |author=Sun_tzu |publisher=joinDota |date=21 June 2013 |access-date=3 July 2014}}</ref> In 2014, four high-profile North American ''Counter-Strike'' players from iBuyPower were suspended from official tournaments after being found guilty of match-fixing, allegedly profiting over US$10,000 through betting on their fixed matches.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/valve-bans-pro-counter-strike-teams-for-match-fixi/1100-6424901/ |title=Valve Bans Pro Counter-Strike Teams For Match Fixing |work=GameSpot |access-date=2 September 2015}}</ref>

[[Skin gambling|Gambling on esports using ''Counter-Strike: Global Offensive'' "skins"]], worth an estimated US$2.3 billion in 2015, came under criticism in June and July 2016 after several questionable legal and ethical aspects were discovered.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-36824689 |title=Valve tackles Counter Strike gambling sites |work=[[BBC]] |date=21 July 2016 |access-date=21 July 2016}}</ref>

===Performance-enhancing drugs===
{{main|Cheating in esports#Doping}}

Reports of widespread use of [[performance-enhancing drugs]] (PEDs) in esports are not uncommon, with players discussing their own, their teammates' and their competitors' use as well as officials acknowledging the prevalence of the issue.<ref name="parkin">{{cite web |last1=Parkin |first1=Simon |title=Winners might use drugs |url=http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2015-04-08-winners-might-use-drugs |access-date=19 July 2015 |website=[[Eurogamer]] |date=8 April 2015}}</ref><ref name="newscientist">{{cite magazine |last1=Hodson |first1=Hal |title=Esports: Doping is rampant, industry insider claims |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn26051-esports-doping-is-rampant-industry-insider-claims#.U-x3KvldU0J |access-date=19 July 2015 |magazine=[[New Scientist]] |date=18 August 2014}}</ref><ref name="summers">{{cite web |last1=Summers |first1=Nick |title=Top 'Counter-Strike' player admits eSports has a doping problem |url=https://www.engadget.com/2015/07/17/esports-adderall-doping/ |access-date=19 July 2015 |publisher=[[Engadget]] |date=17 July 2015}}</ref> Players often turn to [[stimulants]] such as [[Ritalin]], [[Adderall]] and [[Vyvanse]], drugs which can significantly boost concentration, improve reaction time, and prevent fatigue.<ref name="parkin" /> [[Selegiline]], a drug used to treat [[Parkinson's disease]], is reportedly popular, because like stimulants, it enhances mood and motivation. Conversely, drugs with calming effects are also sought after. Some players take [[propranolol]], which blocks the effects of [[adrenaline]], or [[Valium]], which is prescribed to treat [[anxiety disorder]], in order to remain calm under pressure.<ref name="newscientist" /> According to Bjoern Franzen, a former [[SK Gaming]] executive, it is second nature for some ''League of Legends'' players to take as many as three different drugs before competition.<ref name="elephant">{{cite web |last1=Franzen |first1=Bjoern |title=Doping in eSports – The almost invisible Elephant in the room |url=https://bjoernfranzen.com/doping-in-esports-the-almost-invisible-elephant-in-the-room/ |access-date=19 July 2015 |work=BjoernFranzen.com |date=14 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422153147/https://bjoernfranzen.com/doping-in-esports-the-almost-invisible-elephant-in-the-room/ |archive-date=22 April 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> In July 2015 Kory "Semphis" Friesen, an ex-[[Cloud9 (esports)|Cloud9]] player, admitted that he and his teammates were all using Adderall during a match against [[Virtus.pro]] in the [[ESL One Katowice 2015]] ''Counter-Strike: Global Offensive'' tournament, and went on to claim that "everyone" at [[ESEA League]] tournaments uses Adderall.<ref name="summers" /> In 2020, former Call of Duty champion Adam "KiLLa" Sloss told [[The Washington Post]] that one of the major reasons he stopped competing in esports was the "rampant" use of Adderall in the competitive scene.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hamstead |first1=Coleman |title='Nobody talks about it because everyone is on it': Adderall presents esports with an enigma |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/esports/2020/02/13/esports-adderall-drugs/ |newspaper=Washington Post |access-date=23 September 2021 |date=13 February 2021}}</ref>

The unregulated use of such drugs poses severe risks to competitors' health, including [[addiction]], [[overdose]], [[serotonin syndrome]] and, in the case of stimulants, [[weight loss]].<ref name=parkin /><ref name="newscientist" /> Accordingly, Adderall and other such stimulants are banned and their use penalized by many professional sporting bodies and leagues, including [[Major League Baseball]] and the [[National Football League]]. Although [[International e-Sports Federation]] (IeSF) is a signatory of the [[World Anti-Doping Agency]], the governing body has not outlawed any PEDs in its sanctioned competitions.<ref name="parkin" /> Action has been taken on the individual league level, however, as at least one major league, the [[Electronic Sports League]], has made use of any drugs during matches punishable by expulsion from competition.<ref>{{cite web |title=ESL Major Series One Rulebook |url=http://gfx.esl-europe.net/gfx/media/eu/emsone/summer2013/ESL_Major_Series_One_Rulebook.pdf |publisher=[[Electronic Sports League]] |access-date=19 July 2015 |archive-date=22 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150722105358/http://gfx.esl-europe.net/gfx/media/eu/emsone/summer2013/ESL_Major_Series_One_Rulebook.pdf }}</ref> Although not all players use drugs, the use of over-the-counter [[energy drinks]] is common. These energy drinks are often marketed specifically toward gamers, and have also faced media and regulatory scrutiny due to their health risks.<ref name="fuel">{{cite web |last1=Stout |first1=Hilary |title=Selling the Young on 'Gaming Fuel' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/05/20/business/energy-drink-industry-under-scrutiny-looks-to-gamers-to-keep-sales-surging.html |access-date=19 July 2015 |work=The New York Times |date=19 May 2015}}</ref>

===Player exploitation===
There has been some concern over the quality of life and potential mistreatment of players by organizations, especially in South Korea. Korean organizations have been accused of refusing to pay competitive salaries, leading to a slow exodus of Korean players to other markets. In an interview, ''League of Legends'' player Bae "Dade" Eo-jin said that "Korean players wake up at 1 pm and play until 5 am", and suggested that the 16-hour play schedule was a significant factor in causing [[Burnout (psychology)|burnout]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://na.lolesports.com/articles/koreas-pro-exodus-may-spell-bad-news-games-top-region |title=KOREA'S PRO EXODUS MAY SPELL BAD NEWS FOR THE GAME'S TOP REGION |publisher=Riot Games |author=Frank 'Riot Mirhi' Fields |date=5 November 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref> Concerns over the [[mental health]] of players intensified in 2014 when ''League of Legends'' player Cheon "Promise" Min-Ki attempted suicide a week after admitting to [[match fixing]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.polygon.com/2014/3/18/5522192/korean-league-of-legends-player-fixed-matches-suicide |title=Top Korean League of Legends player fixed matches before attempting suicide, says eSports league |website=Polygon |author=Owen S. Good |date=18 March 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref>

To combat the negative environment, Korean ''League of Legends'' teams were given new rules for the upcoming 2015 season by Riot Games, including the adoption of minimum salaries for professional players, requiring contracts and allowing players to stream individually for additional player revenue.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ongamers.com/articles/major-changes-heading-to-korea-for-the-2015-season/1100-2303/ |title=Major changes heading to Korea for the 2015 season |publisher=OnGamers |author=Travis Gafford |date=27 October 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014 |archive-date=10 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151210201355/http://www.ongamers.com/articles/major-changes-heading-to-korea-for-the-2015-season/1100-2303/ }}</ref>

Since esports games often requires many actions per minute, some players may get [[repetitive strain]] injuries, causing hand or wrist pain.<ref>Luke Winkie (31 May 2016) [http://www.vocativ.com/323427/the-esports-injury-crisis/ The eSports Injury Crisis] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180110040656/http://www.vocativ.com/323427/the-esports-injury-crisis/ |date=10 January 2018 }} Vocativ, Retrieved 3 June 2016.</ref> During the early development of the esports industry, sports medicine and gaming-related injuries were ignored by players and organizations, leading to some early player retirements.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Leporati |first1=Gregory |title=Aching wrists, early retirement and the surprising physical toll of esports |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/esports/2022/03/14/professional-esports-athlete-injuries/ |newspaper=Washington Post |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref>

=== Women ===
{{See also|Women and video games}}
The number of female viewers has been growing in esports, with an estimated 30% of esports viewers being female in 2013, a significant increase from 15% the previous year.{{Citation needed|date=January 2017}} However, despite the increase in female viewers, there are still very few female players in high level competitive esports.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kordyaka |first=Bastian |last2=Pumplun |first2=Luisa |last3=Brunnhofer |first3=Marlies |last4=Kruse |first4=Bjoern |last5=Laato |first5=Samuli |date=2023-12-01 |title=Gender disparities in esports – An explanatory mixed-methods approach |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563223003072 |journal=Computers in Human Behavior |volume=149 |article-number=107956 |doi=10.1016/j.chb.2023.107956 |issn=0747-5632|doi-access=free }}</ref> As of 2024, 33% of European e-sports viewers are female.<ref>{{Cite web |date=Dec 2024 |title=Let's Play! 2024: The esports market |url=https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/assets-zone2/de/de/docs/industries/technology-media-telecommunications/2024/Deloitte-Lets-Play-Esports-final-%202024.pdf |access-date=1 Jan 2026 |website=Deloitte}}</ref> The top female players that are involved in esports mainly get exposure in female-only tournaments, most notably ''Counter-Strike'', ''[[Dead or Alive 4]]'', and ''StarCraft II''. Current all-female esports teams include [[Frag Dolls]] and [[PMS Clan]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2017}}

The formation of Team Siren, an all-female ''[[League of Legends]]'' team, in June 2013 was met with controversy and dismissed as a "gimmick" to attract men's attention.<ref>{{cite web |date=30 May 2013 |title=Introducing Team Siren – YouTube |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Gz9um3wV1o |website=[[YouTube]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=10 June 2013 |title=Why Team Siren Matters |url=http://www.rtsguru.com/game/435/article/5991/Why-Team-Siren-Matters.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924092521/http://www.rtsguru.com/game/435/article/5991/Why-Team-Siren-Matters.html |archive-date=24 September 2015 |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref> The team disbanded within a month due to negative publicity from their promotional video and the team captain's poor attitude towards her teammates.<ref>{{cite web |date=19 June 2013 |title=Siren broke up (with proof) – Page 16 – League of Legends Community |url=http://forums.na.leagueoflegends.com/board/showthread.php?p=38929204#post38929204 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170311162545/http://forums.na.leagueoflegends.com/board/showthread.php?p=38929204#post38929204 |archive-date=11 March 2017 |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=26 June 2013 |title=League of Legends Team Siren Disbands: Valuable Lessons Learned – League of Legends |url=http://www.gameskinny.com/hzi5j/league-of-legends-team-siren-disbands-valuable-lessons-learned |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref> In 2018, [[Vaevictis Esports|Team Vaevictis]] attempted to field an all-female roster in the [[League of Legends Continental League|LCL]], the top esports league in Russia,<ref>{{cite tweet |number=1094686736570032132 |user=VaevictisTeam |title=We're proud to present you Vaevictis eSports roster for LCL Spring 2019! |author=Vaevictis eSports |date=10 February 2019 |access-date=3 June 2019}}</ref> but faced similar criticism.<ref>{{cite news |date=17 February 2019 |title=All-female Russian LoL team Vaevictis Esports lose 52–2 in the LCL: Is this really about giving women a platform or is it just an unfair publicity stunt? |url=https://esports-news.co.uk/2019/02/17/vaevictis-esports-all-female-team/ |access-date=3 June 2019 |work=Esports News UK}}</ref> Vaevictis went 0–14 in both splits, and in February 2020, the LCL announced their disbandment due to a failure to field a competitive roster.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 February 2020 |title=League of Legends: Vaevictis eSports removed from LCL due to poor results |url=https://www.millenium.gg/news/12786.html |access-date=25 November 2020 |website=Millenium US |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Vaevictis female roster removed from LCL |url=https://www.earlygame.com/vaevictis-female-roster-experiment-ends-in-expulsion-from-lcl/ |access-date=25 November 2020 |website=EarlyGame |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=17 February 2020 |title=League of Legends: All-female team Vaevictis kicked out of LCL due to poor performance; CrowCrowd, owned by former player Likkrit joins the league |url=https://www.invenglobal.com/articles/10417/all-female-team-vaevictis-kicked-out-of-lcl-due-to-poor-performance-crowcrowd-owned-by-former-player-likkrit-joins-the-league |access-date=25 November 2020 |website=InvenGlobal |language=en}}</ref> The LCL stated, "The results of the 2019 season showed a huge difference in Vaevictis Esports' results compared to other LCL teams, which is an unacceptable level of competitiveness in a franchised league."

===Economics===
The [[League of Legends Championship Series|''League of Legends'' Championship Series]] and [[League of Legends Champions Korea|''League of Legends'' Champions Korea]] offer guaranteed [[salaries]] for players.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newsoflegends.com/index.php/official-2015-season-lol-esports-league-reform-plan-announced-final-version-29648/ |title=Official 2015 Season LoL eSports League Reform Plan Announced (Final Version) |website=News of Legends |date=11 November 2014 |author=Caymus |access-date=28 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518084152/http://www.newsoflegends.com/index.php/official-2015-season-lol-esports-league-reform-plan-announced-final-version-29648/ |archive-date=18 May 2015 }}</ref> Despite this, online streaming is preferred by some players, as in some cases, streaming can be more profitable than competing with a team, and streamers have the ability to determine their own schedule. The International tournament awards US$10 million to the winners, however teams that do not have the same amount of success often do not have financial stability and frequently break up after failing to win.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailydot.com/esports/dota-2-prize-distribution-players/ |title=Dota 2 is the richest of the big esports, but its players are the poorest |date=13 August 2014 |website=[[The Daily Dot]] |access-date=2 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518071207/http://www.dailydot.com/esports/dota-2-prize-distribution-players/ |archive-date=18 May 2015 }}</ref>

In 2015 it was estimated by SuperData Research, that the global esports industry generated revenue of around US$748.8 million that year. Asia is the leading esports market with over $321 million in revenue, with North America at around $224 million, and Europe at $172 million. For comparison, the rest of the world combines for approximately $29 million.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://fortune.com/2015/10/28/global-esports-revenues-nearing-2-billion/ |title=Global esports revenues are nearing 2 billion |first=John |last=Gaudiosi |website=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]] |date=28 October 2015 |access-date=9 November 2015}}</ref> Global esports revenue is estimated to reach $1.9 billion by 2018. During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], the video gaming industry bypassed many economic sectors by providing a means of compensating for the physical isolation imposed by the lockdown, transforming it into an increasingly important economic sector within the global economy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Resolving Video Games and eSports Disputes: How Can WIPO Alternative Dispute Resolution Options Help? |url=https://www.wipo.int/wipo_magazine_digital/en/2023/article_0018.html |website=WIPO Magazine}}</ref>

===Gambling===
{{expand section|date=June 2018}}
{{main|Esports betting}}

Gambling on esports matches have historically been illegal or unregulated by major markets. This created a [[black market]] via virtual currency. In places where esports gambling is not officially recognized, the lack of regulation has resulted in match-fixing by players or third parties, and created issues with underage gambling due to the draw of video games. Some games allow bets in their [[in-game currency]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotaku.com/dota-2-now-lets-you-bet-in-game-currency-on-pro-tournam-1833502199|title=Dota 2 Now Lets You Bet In-Game Currency On Pro Tournaments|website=Kotaku|date=22 March 2019 |language=en-us|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref> while third-party gambling platforms will often take bets placed using virtual items earned in games.<ref name="wapost betting"/> In esports gambling, most bets and odds are structured in the same way as traditional sports. Most gambling sites offering the booker service allow users to bet based on the outcome of tournaments, matches or special esports titles. On the other hand, due to the nature of esports, there are numerous innovative ways to make bets, which are based on in-game milestones.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://venturebeat.com/2019/06/03/betting-is-esports-biggest-and-most-underappreciated-opportunity/|title=Betting is esports' biggest and most underappreciated opportunity|date=3 June 2019|website=VentureBeat|language=en-US|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref> For example, [[League of Legends|League of Legend]] bettors may place their money on which team/champion will take the "First Blood".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lolbettingsites.com/lol-esports-bets/|title=LoL esports bets explained ➠ Best esports advice|website=LoLBettingSites.com|language=en-US|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref>

Esports gambling in the United States has been illegal under the federal [[Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act of 1992]] (PASPA). The Act prevented all but five states from allowing gambling on sporting events.<ref name="wapost betting"/> However, regulation of esports betting still depended on state law. Some betting houses in Nevada, where sports betting has been already exempted under PASPA, classify esports as non-competitive "other events" similar to the selection of the [[Heisman Trophy]] winner or [[NFL draft]] which are considered as legal.<ref name="wapost betting">{{cite news | title = Esports bookmaking? Globally, it's already a billion-dollar gambling industry |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/sports/breaking/ct-esports-bookmaking-20180406-story.html|first = Noah | last = Smith | date = 6 April 2018 | access-date = 8 June 2018 | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] }}</ref> Other companies established in the United States allow betting on esports to international users but are restricted to Americans. Nevada legalized esports gambling in June 2017, classifying esports along with competitive sports and dog racing.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.espn.com/chalk/story/_/id/19512317/chalk-nevada-governor-approves-esports-betting-bill | title = Nevada governor approves esports betting bill | first = Jacob | last = Wolf | date = 2 June 2017 | access-date = 8 June 2018 | work = [[ESPN]] }}</ref> With the [[Supreme Court of the United States]]'s ruling in ''[[Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association]]'' in May 2018, PASPA was recognized as unconstitutional, as the Court claimed that the federal government cannot limit states from regulating [[sports betting]]. This created the potential for legalized esports-based betting in the United States.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamesn.com/esports-betting | title = Esports betting may soon become legal in several American states | first = Ali | last= Jones | date = 17 May 2018 | access-date=8 June 2018 | work = [[PCGamesN]] }}</ref> However, New Jersey, the state at the center of the Supreme Court case, passed its bill to legalize sports gambling but restricted gambling on esports to only international competitions where most players are over 18 years of age.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://compete.kotaku.com/new-jersey-added-a-last-minute-esports-betting-ban-and-1826678155 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180610091914/https://compete.kotaku.com/new-jersey-added-a-last-minute-esports-betting-ban-and-1826678155 | archive-date = 10 June 2018 | title = New Jersey Added A Last-Minute Esports Betting Ban And No One Knows Why | first = Maddy | last= Myers | date = 8 June 2018 | access-date = 8 June 2018 | work = [[Kotaku]] }}</ref> Without PASPA, interstate gambling on esports would be still be limited by the [[Federal Wire Act]], preventing users from betting on national esports events outside of the state.<ref name="wapost betting"/>

In 2019, the countries where esports gambling is legal include the UK, New Zealand, Australia, China, Spain, Canada, South Korea, and Japan, and many of them are the international hosts for gaming tournaments.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gamopo.com/countries/|title=Esports Betting Laws & Country Restrictions 2019 {{!}} Gamopo Esports Hub|website=Gamopo.com|language=en-US|access-date=5 September 2019}}</ref> By the end of 2019, the state of [[New Jersey]] approved esports betting, just in time for the finals of the LoL Worlds Cup 2019 final match, which had over 4.000.000 spectators.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.esports.net/news/industry/new-jersey-allows-esports-betting-in-time-for-league-of-legends-final/|title=New Jersey Allows Esports Betting in Time for League of Legends Final|date=12 November 2019|website=Esports.net|language=en-US|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref>

The esports [[gambling industry]] has attracted criticism because of its target audience. As a large part of the esports audience is underage, governments and regulators have expressed skepticism regarding the market and the possibility of underage gambling. Additionally, gambling platforms have received criticism for their integration with the larger esports industry.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bräutigam |first1=Thiemo |title=Is it a problem that esports betting sites are sponsoring teams? – ARCHIVE – The Esports Observer |url=https://archive.esportsobserver.com/is-it-a-problem-that-esports-betting-sites-are-sponsoring-teams/ |website=Esports Observer |access-date=21 March 2022 |date=24 September 2015}}</ref> Esports platforms regularly sponsor professional esports teams, as happened with the contract between [[Betway]] and [[PSG.LGD]] team ([[Dota 2]]) in August 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://medium.com/instant-sponsor/betway-partners-with-psg-lgd-and-gains-control-over-team-branding-a447c8abb301|title=Betway Partners With PSG.LGD And Gains Control Over Team Branding|last=Kuchefski|first=Kathryn|date=14 August 2019|website=Medium|language=en|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref>

===Data analytics and machine learning===
With the growing popularity of [[machine learning]] in data analytics,{{Citation needed|date=November 2018}} esports has been the focus of several software programs that analyze the plethora of game data available. Based on the huge number of matches played on a daily basis globally ([[League of Legends]] alone had a reported 100 million active monthly players worldwide in 2016<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.riftherald.com/2016/9/13/12865314/monthly-lol-players-2016-active-worldwide | title = Number of players of selected eSports games worldwide as of August 2017 (in million) | date = 13 September 2016 | access-date=12 August 2018 | work = [[Rift Herald]] }}</ref> and an average of 27 million League of Legends games played per day reported in 2014<ref>Sheer, Ian (27 January 2014). "Player Tally for 'League of Legends' Surges". Wsj.com. Archived from the original on 30 January 2014. Retrieved 31 January 2014.</ref>), these games can be used for applying big-data machine learning platforms. Several games make their data publicly available, so websites aggregate the data into easy-to-visualize graphs and statistics. In addition, several programs use machine learning tools to predict the win probability of a match based on various factors, such as team composition.<ref>{{cite arXiv | title = Win Prediction in Esports: Mixed-Rank Match Prediction in Multi-player Online Battle Arena Games | date = 17 November 2017 |eprint = 1711.06498|last1 = Hodge|first1 = Victoria|last2 = Devlin|first2 = Sam|last3 = Sephton|first3 = Nick|last4 = Block|first4 = Florian|last5 = Drachen|first5 = Anders|last6 = Cowling|first6 = Peter|class = cs.AI}}</ref> In 2018, the [[DotA]] team [[Team Liquid]] partnered with a software company to allow players and coaches to predict the team's success rate in each match and provide advice on what needs to be changed to improve performance.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.abs-cbn.com/sports/05/10/18/dota-analytics-big-data-meets-e-sports-in-software-giant-deal-with-team-liquid | title = 'DOTA analytics': Big data meets e-sports in software giant deal with Team Liquid | date = 10 May 2018 | access-date=12 August 2018 | work = [[ABS-CBN News]] }}</ref>

===Game cancellations===
As more esports competitions and leagues are run entirely or in portion by the video game publisher or developer for the game, the ongoing viability of that game's esports activities is tied to that company. In December 2018, Blizzard announced that it was reducing resources spent on the development of ''Heroes of the Storm'' and canceling its plans for tournaments in 2019. This caused several professional ''Heroes'' players and coaches to recognize that their career was no longer viable, and expressed outrage and disappointment at Blizzard's decision.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.engadget.com/2018/12/14/blizzard-ends-heroes-of-the-storm-esports/| title= Blizzard cancels 'Heroes of the Storm' eSports plans | first =Saqid | last = Shah | date = 14 December 2018 | access-date = 16 December 2018 | work = [[Engadget]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2018/12/14/18141331/heroes-of-the-storm-canceled-hgc-blizzard-community | title = Heroes of the Storm pros vent sadness, anger after Blizzard kills game's esports future | first = Michael | last= McWhertor | date = 14 December 2018 | access-date = 16 December 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] }}</ref>

==Media coverage==
{{multiple image|image1=The International 2018 (30302304258).jpg|image2=The International 2018 (30302303908).jpg|footer=As with traditional sporting events, larger esport events, such as [[The International (Dota 2)|The International]], usually feature live pre- and post-game discussion by a panel of analysts (''top''), with in-match casting being done by [[play-by-play]] and [[color commentators]] (''bottom'').|width=250|direction=vertical|align=right}}

===News reporting===
The main medium for esports coverage is the [[Internet]]. In the mid-2010s, mainstream sports and news reporting websites, such as ''[[ESPN]]'', ''[[Yahoo!]]'', ''[[Sport1 (Germany)|Sport1]]'', ''[[Kicker (magazine)|Kicker]]'', and ''[[Aftonbladet]]'' started dedicated esports coverage.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dave |first1=Paresh |title=ESPN.com to cover e-sports with same 'rigor' as it does the big leagues |url=http://www.latimes.com/business/technology/la-fi-tn-espn-esports-20160113-story.html |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |access-date=13 July 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Yahoo Launches New Experience Dedicated to Esports |url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/yahoo-launches-experience-dedicated-esports-050000022.html |website=Yahoo |access-date=13 July 2016}}</ref> Esports tournaments commonly use commentators or casters to provide live commentary of games in progress, similar to a traditional [[sports commentator]]. For popular casters, providing commentary for esports can be a full-time position by itself.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.polygon.com/features/2013/7/16/4503412/starcraft-commentators-tastosis |title=How two StarCraft commentators became stars |website=Polygon |author=Tracey Lien |date=16 July 2013 |access-date=11 September 2013}}</ref> Prominent casters for ''StarCraft II'' include [[Dan "Artosis" Stemkoski]] and [[Nick "Tasteless" Plott]]. However, the impact of [[COVID-19 pandemic]] affected how esports were covered in addition to the sports themselves. Notably, ''ESPN''{{'s}} dedicated esports coverage was shuttered in November 2020 as the network refocus on more traditional sports, though said they would still have some coverage of esports events.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/esports/2021/02/16/espn-esports/ | title = The rise, fall and resonance of ESPN Esports | first = Noah | last = Smith | date = 16 February 2021 | access-date = 18 October 2021 | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] }}</ref>

In 2018, the [[Associated Press]]' [[AP Stylebook]] officially began spelling the word as "esports", dropping support for both the capital "S" and the dash between "e" and "sports" styles, similar to how "[[e-mail]]" transformed with common usage to "email".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://dotesports.com/culture/ap-style-esports-13789 |title=Goodbye eSports: The 2017 AP Style Guide will settle the esports spelling debate once and for all |publisher=Dot Esports |author=Justin Binkowski |date=25 March 2017 |access-date=26 April 2017 |archive-date=19 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170519175625/https://dotesports.com/culture/ap-style-esports-13789 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://esports.yahoo.com/its-official-the-ap-style-guide-spells-it-esports-not-esports-e-sports-or-esports-233434245.html |title=It's official: The AP Style guide spells it 'esports', not 'eSports', 'e-sports', or 'Esports' |publisher=Yahoo Esports |author=Taylor Cocke |date=24 March 2017}}</ref> Richard Tyler Blevins, better known as "[[Ninja (streamer)|Ninja]]", became the first professional gamer to appear in a cover story for a major sports magazine when he appeared in the September 2018 issue of ''[[ESPN The Magazine]]''.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.vg247.com/2018/09/18/ninja-espn-magazine-cover/ | title = Fortnite streamer Ninja graces cover of latest ESPN magazine – a first for professional gaming | first = Stephany | last = Nunnelley | date = 18 September 2018 | access-date = 18 September 2018 | work = [[VG247]] }}</ref>

===Internet live streaming===
[[File:Vikkikitty at 2GGaming Championship Saga.jpg|thumb|right|In January 2017, [[Victoria Perez]] (pictured in December 2017), also known as VikkiKitty, was the first woman to commentate a major ''[[Super Smash Bros.]]'' event.]]
Many esports events are [[streamed]] online to viewers over the internet. With the shutdown of the Own3d streaming service in 2013, [[Twitch (service)|Twitch]] is by far the most popular streaming service for esports, competing against other providers such as Hitbox.tv, Azubu, and [[YouTube Gaming]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.redbull.com/en/games/stories/1331687386855/hitbox-vs-twitch-which-is-better |title=How Hitbox plans to take on Twitch |author=Jon Partridge |publisher=RedBull |date=29 October 2014 |access-date=29 October 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamingsoul.com/pcmac/own3d-is-shutting-down-twitch-tv-declared-winner/ |title=Own3D is Shutting Down. Twitch Declared Winner. |publisher=GamingSoul |author=Erik Cloutier |date=29 January 2013 |access-date=1 July 2013}}</ref> Dreamhack Winter 2011 reached 1.7 million unique viewers on Twitch.<ref name="dreamhackrecord">{{cite web |url=http://www.dreamhack.se/dhw11/2011/12/06/dreamhack-and-twitch-tv-announce-record-breaking-online-viewership/ |title=Dreamhack and Twitch Announce Record-Breaking Online Viewership |date=16 April 2021 |publisher=Dreamhack}}</ref> While coverage of live events usually brings in the largest viewership counts, the recent popularization of streaming services has allowed individuals to broadcast their own gameplay independent of such events as well. Individual broadcasters can enter an agreement with Twitch or Hitbox in which they receive a portion of the advertisement revenue from commercials which run on the stream they create.<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/insertcoin/2013/02/05/talking-livestreams-esports-and-the-future-of-entertainment-with-twitch-tv/ |title=Talking Livestreams, eSports and the Future of Entertainment with Twitch |author=Paul Tassi |magazine=Forbes |date=2 May 2013 |access-date=16 September 2013}}</ref>

Another major streaming platform was [[Major League Gaming]]'s MLG.tv.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://tv.majorleaguegaming.com/ |title=MLG Streaming Platform |publisher=Major League Gaming |access-date=28 July 2014 |archive-date=9 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140709141832/http://tv.majorleaguegaming.com/ }}</ref> The network, which specializes in ''[[Call of Duty]]'' content but hosts a range of gaming titles, has seen increasing popularity, with 1376% growth in MLG.tv viewership in Q1 of 2014.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.majorleaguegaming.com/news/nadeshot-joins-mlg-tv-streaming-platform-apps-for-android-and-ios-released |title=1376% Growth in MLG.tv Viewership in Q1 |publisher=Major League Gaming |date=10 April 2014 |access-date=28 June 2013 |archive-date=13 July 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170713090243/http://www.majorleaguegaming.com/news/nadeshot-joins-mlg-tv-streaming-platform-apps-for-android-and-ios-released/ }}</ref> The 2014 ''[[Call of Duty: Ghosts]]'' broadcast at [[Major League Gaming|MLG]]'s X Games event drew over 160,000 unique viewers.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.esportsmax.com/events/mlg-championship-2014-anaheim-ca |title=MLG Championship 2014 – Anaheim, CA |publisher=Esports Maxl |date=22 June 2014 |access-date=28 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140627135654/http://www.esportsmax.com/events/mlg-championship-2014-anaheim-ca |archive-date=27 June 2014 }}</ref> The network, like Twitch, allows users to broadcast themselves playing games, though only select individuals can use the service. For several years, MLG.tv was the primary streaming platform for the ''[[Call of Duty]]'' professional scene; famous players such as [[NaDeSHoT]] and [[Scump]] have signed contracts with the company to use its streaming service exclusively.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.majorleaguegaming.com/news/nadeshot-joins-mlg-tv-streaming-platform-apps-for-android-and-ios-released |title=Video Game Super Star "Nadeshot" Signs Exclusive Deal with Major League Gaming |publisher=Major League Gaming |date=10 April 2014 |access-date=28 June 2013 |archive-date=13 July 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170713090243/http://www.majorleaguegaming.com/news/nadeshot-joins-mlg-tv-streaming-platform-apps-for-android-and-ios-released/ }}</ref> In January 2016, MLG was acquired by [[Activision Blizzard]].<ref name="nyt-mlgbuy" />

[[YouTube]] also relaunched its livestreaming platform with a renewed focus on live gaming and esports specifically.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailydot.com/esports/youtube-google-esports-livestreaming/ |title=YouTube to relaunch livestreaming service with focus on esports and gaming |first=Richard |last=Lewis |website=The Daily Dot |date=24 March 2015 |access-date=4 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150414052737/http://www.dailydot.com/esports/youtube-google-esports-livestreaming/ |archive-date=14 April 2015 }}</ref> For [[The International 2014]], coverage was also simulcast on [[ESPN]]'s streaming service [[ESPN3]].<ref name="polygon-espn3dota">{{cite web |url=http://www.polygon.com/2014/7/17/5913301/the-international-dota-2-championships-espn3 |title=The International Dota 2 championships will be watchable on ESPN3 |work=Polygon |date=17 July 2014 |access-date=21 July 2014}}</ref> In December 2016, [[Riot Games]] announced a deal with [[MLB Advanced Media]]'s technology division BAM Tech for the company to distribute and monetize broadcasts of ''League of Legends'' events through 2023. BAM Tech will pay Riot at least $300 million per-year, and split advertising revenue.<ref name="polygon-bamtechaol">{{cite web |title=League of Legends' maker inks rich broadcast contract, with an eye on premium content |url=http://www.polygon.com/2016/12/18/13998614/league-of-legends-premium-tv-service-mlb |website=Polygon |date=18 December 2016 |publisher=Vox Media |access-date=18 December 2016}}</ref><ref name="wsj-lolmlb">{{cite news |title='League of Legends' E-Sports Contests Lure Newest Fan: Major League Baseball |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/league-of-legends-e-sports-contests-lure-newest-fan-major-league-baseball-1481889603 |website=The Wall Street Journal |date=16 December 2016 |access-date=18 December 2016|last1=Needleman |first1=Sarah E. }}</ref>

===Television===
[[File:Televised Star Craft.jpg|thumb|left|''[[StarCraft]]'' match televised on [[MBCGame]] in [[Seoul]], South Korea]]

Especially since the popularization of streaming in esports, organizations no longer prioritize television coverage, preferring online streaming websites such as [[Twitch (service)|Twitch]]. [[Ongamenet]] continues to broadcast as an esports channel in South Korea, but [[MBCGame]] was taken off the air in 2012. Riot Games' Dustin Beck stated that "TV's not a priority or a goal",<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/danieltack/2013/09/04/riot-games-league-of-legends-and-the-future-of-esports/ |title=Riot Games, 'League of Legends', And The Future Of eSports |magazine=Forbes |author=Daniel Tack |date=4 September 2013 |access-date=8 October 2013}}</ref> and DreamHack's Tomas Hermansson said "esports have [been proven] to be successful on internet streaming [services]."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gosugamers.net/starcraft2/news/25446-dreamhack-partners-with-mtg-for-esports-studio-in-stockholm |title=DreamHack partners with MTG for eSports studio in Stockholm |publisher=Gosu Gamers |author=Radoslav "Nydra" Kolev |date=25 September 2013 |access-date=12 November 2013}}</ref>

On the night before the finals of [[The International 2014]] in August, [[ESPN3]] broadcast a half-hour special profiling the tournament.<ref name="polygon-espn3dota"/> In 2015, ESPN2 broadcast ''Heroes of the Dorm'', the grand finals of the ''[[Heroes of the Storm]]'' collegiate tournament. The first-place team from the [[University of California, Berkeley]] received tuition for each of the team's players, paid for by Blizzard and Tespa.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Molina |first1=Brett |title=Blizzard unveils "Heroes of the Storm" tournament |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/gaming/2015/03/06/heroes-of-the-storm-tournament/24493989/ |website=USA Today |access-date=24 January 2016}}</ref> The top four teams won gaming equipment and new computers. This was the first time an esport had ever been broadcast on a major American television network. The broadcast was an attempt to broaden the appeal of esports by reaching viewers who would not normally come across it. However, the broadcast was met with a few complaints. Those living outside of the United States were unable to view the tournament. Additionally, the tournament could not be viewed online via streams, cutting off a large portion of viewers from the main demographic in the process.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pcgamer.com/heroes-of-the-dorm-finals-were-a-success-story-for-esports/ |title=Heroes of the Dorm finals were a success story for esports |website=[[PCGamer]] |first=Tom |last=Marks |date=27 April 2015 |access-date=4 May 2015}}</ref>

In September 2015, [[Turner Broadcasting System|Turner Broadcasting]] partnered with [[William Morris Endeavor|WME/IMG]]. In December 2015, the partnered companies announced two seasons of the [[ELeague]], a [[Counter-Strike: Global Offensive]] league based in North America including 15 teams from across the world competing for a $1,200,000 prize pool each 10-week season. The tournament, filmed at Turner's studios in [[Atlanta]], Georgia, was simultaneously streamed on online streaming websites and [[TBS (U.S. TV channel)|TBS]] on Friday nights.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.e-league.com/|title=ELeague Official Website|access-date=27 January 2016|archive-date=22 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160822190032/http://www.e-league.com/}}</ref>

In January 2016, [[Activision Blizzard]], publishers of the ''Call of Duty'' and ''StarCraft'' series, acquired [[Major League Gaming]]. In an interview with ''[[The New York Times]]'' about the purchase, Activision Blizzard CEO [[Bobby Kotick]] explained that the company was aspiring to create a U.S. cable network devoted to esports, which he described as "the ESPN of video games". He felt that higher quality productions, more in line with those of traditional sports telecasts, could help to broaden the appeal of esports to advertisers. Activision Blizzard had hired former ESPN and [[NFL Network]] executive [[Steve Bornstein]] to be CEO of the company's esports division.<ref name="nyt-mlgbuy">{{cite news |title=Activision Buys Major League Gaming to Broaden Role in E-Sports |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/01/05/technology/activision-buys-major-league-gaming-to-broaden-role-in-e-sports.html?smid=tw-share&_r=1 |website=The New York Times |date = 4 January 2016|access-date=5 January 2016|last1 = Wingfield|first1 = Nick}}</ref>

[[TV 2 (Norway)|TV 2]], the largest private television broadcaster in [[Norway]], broadcasts esports across the country. TV 2 partnered with local Norwegian organization House of Nerds to bring a full season of esports competition with an initial lineup of ''Counter-Strike: Global Offensive'', ''League of Legends'', and ''StarCraft II''.<ref>Commercial broadcast company TV 2 is partnering with local Norwegian organization House of Nerds to bring a full season of esports competition to domestic airwaves.</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailydot.com/esports/esports-norway-tv2/ |title=Esports are coming to television in Norway |website=[[The Daily Dot]] |first=Jared |last=Wynne |date=18 February 2015 |access-date=7 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150414000347/http://www.dailydot.com/esports/esports-norway-tv2/ |archive-date=14 April 2015 }}</ref>

In April 2016, [[Big Ten Network]] announced a collaboration with Riot to hold an invitational ''League of Legends'' competition between two universities from the collegiate [[Big Ten Conference]], as part of Riot's collegiate championships at [[PAX East]].<ref name="sbnation-btnlol">{{cite web |title=Riot Games and Big Ten Network partner for televised Ohio State vs. Michigan State League of Legends match |date=14 April 2016 |url=https://www.sbnation.com/2016/4/14/11414260/ohio-state-michigan-state-league-of-legends-big-ten-network |publisher=[[SB Nation]] |access-date=18 April 2016}}</ref> On 17 January 2017, Big Ten Network and Riot announced that it would hold a larger season of conference competition involving 10 Big Ten schools.<ref name="nyt-big10lol">{{cite news |title=Big Ten Universities Entering a New Realm: E-Sports |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/01/19/sports/big-ten-is-entering-a-new-realm-e-sports.html |website=The New York Times |date=19 January 2017 |access-date=27 January 2017|last1=Tracy |first1=Marc }}</ref>

[[Nielsen Holdings]], a global information company known for tracking viewership for television and other media, announced in August 2017 that it would launch Nielsen esports, a division devoted to providing similar viewership and other consumer research data around esports, forming an advisory board with members from [[ESL (company)|ESL]], [[Activision Blizzard]], [[Twitch (service)|Twitch]], [[YouTube]], [[ESPN]], and [[FIFA]] to help determine how to track and monitor audience sizes for esports events.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/nielsen-esports-company |title=The company that governs TV ratings just started an esports organisation |first=Ali |last=Jones |date=18 August 2017 |access-date=18 August 2017 |work=[[PCGamesN]]}}</ref>

In July 2018, on the first day of the inaugural [[2018 Overwatch League season]] playoffs, Blizzard and [[Disney]] announced a multi-year deal that gave Disney and its networks [[ESPN]] and [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] broadcast rights to the Overwatch League and [[Overwatch World Cup]], starting with the playoffs and continuing with future events.<ref name="OWL on TV">{{cite web | url = http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/24062274/overwatch-league-comes-espn-disney-abc | title = Overwatch League comes to ESPN, Disney and ABC | date = 11 July 2018 | access-date = 11 July 2018 | work = [[ESPN]] }}</ref>
