Teams such as [[FaZe Clan]], [[Cloud9]], [[Fnatic]], [[T1 (esports)|T1]], [[G2 Esports]], and [[Natus Vincere]] have become successful within esports and now sponsor esports players around the world.<ref name="Forbes-Most-Valuable">{{cite web |last1=Knight |first1=Brett |title=The Most Valuable Esports Companies 2022 |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/brettknight/2022/05/06/the-most-valuable-esports-companies-2022/?sh=3e094ec9599f |website=Forbes |access-date=27 March 2023 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Chalk |first1=Andy |title=Ukrainian esports team Na'Vi says it is 'not going to leave the country' |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/ukrainian-esports-team-navi-says-it-is-not-going-to-leave-the-country/ |website=PC Gamer |access-date=27 March 2023 |language=en |date=12 March 2022}}</ref> These teams often cover multiple esports games within tournaments and leagues, with various team makeups for each game. They may also represent single players for one-on-one esports games like fighting games within [[Evolution Championship Series]], or ''Hearthstone'' tournaments. In addition to prize money from tournament wins, players in these teams and associations may also be paid a separate team salary. Team sponsorship may cover tournament travel expenses or gaming hardware. Prominent esports sponsors include companies such as [[Logitech]] and [[Razer Inc.|Razer]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.esfiworld.com/interview-with-razers-global-e-sports-manager-the-business-behind-sponsoring-teams/ |title=Interview with Razer's global e-sports manager: The business behind sponsoring teams |author=Brent Ruiz |date=3 February 2013 |publisher=ESFI World |access-date=10 September 2013 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130822230651/http://www.esfiworld.com/interview-with-razers-global-e-sports-manager-the-business-behind-sponsoring-teams/ |archive-date=22 August 2013 }}</ref> Teams feature these sponsors on their website, team jerseys and on their social media, in 2016 the biggest teams have social media followings of over a million.<ref>{{cite web |title=OpTic Gaming™ (@OpTicGaming) {{!}} Twitter|url=https://twitter.com/OpTicGaming|website=twitter.com|access-date=27 January 2016}}</ref> Associations include the [[Korea e-Sports Association]] (KeSPA), the [[International Esports Federation]] (IESF), the [[British Esports|British Esports Federation]], and the [[World Esports Association]] (WESA).

Some traditional sporting athletes have invested in esports, such as [[Rick Fox]]'s ownership of [[Echo Fox]],<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-12-18/former-nba-player-rick-fox-buys-esports-team-gravity |title=Former NBA Player Rick Fox Buys eSports Team Gravity |first=Scott |last=Soshnick |newspaper=Bloomberg.com |publisher=[[Bloomberg News]] |date=18 December 2015 |access-date=18 December 2015}}</ref> [[Jeremy Lin]]'s ownership of [[Team VGJ]],<ref>{{cite web|last1=Van Allen|first1=Eric|title=Jeremy Lin endorses new Dota 2 team VGJ|url=http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/17579673/jeremy-lin-endorse-new-dota-2-team-vgj|website=ESPN|date=18 September 2016|access-date=5 October 2016}}</ref> and [[Shaquille O'Neal]]'s investment in [[NRG Esports]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/17209251/shaq-nrg-esports-pick-overwatch-team |title=Shaq, NRG Esports pick up Overwatch team |date=3 August 2016 |publisher=ESPN}}</ref> Some association football teams, such as [[FC Schalke 04]] in Germany,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/15552685/soccer-org-schalke-04-finalizes-league-championship-series-roster-picks-fox |title=Sources: Soccer org Schalke 04 finalizes League Championship Series roster, picks up Fox |work=espn.com|date=15 May 2016 }}</ref> [[PSG Esports|Paris Saint-Germain]] in France;<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.espnfc.com/paris-saint-germain/story/2977336/psg-unveil-first-three-signings-in-ambitious-esports-venture |title=PSG unveil first three signings in ambitious eSports venture |first=Jonathan |last=Johnson |date=20 October 2016 |access-date=5 November 2016 |publisher=ESPN}}</ref> [[Beşiktaş J.K.]], [[Fenerbahçe S.K.]], and [[Galatasaray S.K.]] in Turkey; [[Panathinaikos F.C.]] in Greece either sponsor or have complete ownership in esports teams.<ref>{{cite web |title=Espor nedir? Bora Koçyiğit Fanatik'e anlattı!|url=http://www.fanatik.com.tr/2017/04/06/espor-nedir-bora-kocyigit-fanatik-e-anlatti-1286961|access-date=17 January 2018}}</ref>

Competitive esports tournaments in the most popular games pay hundreds to thousands of dollars to players for winning tournaments.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fang |first=Ben Westcott, Nanlin |date=31 December 2019 |title=They train 14 hours a day, 7 days a week, chasing million-dollar paydays. Meet China's new breed of esports athletes {{!}} CNN Business |url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/12/30/tech/chinese-gamers-competition-intl-hnk/index.html |access-date=13 February 2023 |website=CNN |language=en}}</ref> ''[[Dota 2]]''{{'}}s 2021 tournament [[The International (Dota 2)|The International]] had a prize pool over $40 million, the largest in esports history, thanks to its Compendium battle pass contributing a portion of its sales to it. ''[[Counter-Strike: Global Offensive]]'' had a total 2021 prize pool, across all tournaments, of around $22 million.<ref>{{Cite web |title=5 Highest Paying Esports Games in 2022 - Gaming.net |url=https://www.gaming.net/5-highest-paying-esports-games-in-2022/ |access-date=25 February 2023 |website=www.gaming.net}}</ref> The current biggest esports tournament by prize pool, the King Pro League Grand Finals for ''[[Honor of Kings]]'', provides just under US$10 million for the twelve teams that take part.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Chen |first1=Hongyu |title=Tencent's King Pro League Grand Finals to Feature $10M Prize Pool |url=https://esportsadvocate.net/2024/09/tencents-king-pro-league-grand-finals-to-feature-10m-prize-pool/ |access-date=November 11, 2024 |work=The Esports Advocate |date=September 20, 2024}}</ref> However, financial security in the industry is largely limited to players in top performing teams. One study found that only 1 in 5 professional gamers have careers that last longer than two years.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ward |first1=Michael R. |last2=Harmon |first2=Alexander D. |date=December 2019 |title=ESport Superstars |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1527002519859417 |journal=Journal of Sports Economics |language=en |volume=20 |issue=8 |pages=987–1013 |doi=10.1177/1527002519859417 |s2cid=219387589 |issn=1527-0025|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Team rosters are extremely volatile, sometimes changing players or rosters within a season.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Justice |first1=Glen |title=Professional Video Gaming |url=https://library.cqpress.com/cqresearcher/document.php?id=cqresrre2023030300 |journal=CQ Researcher |access-date=27 March 2023 |pages=1–19 |date=3 March 2023|volume=33 |issue=8 }}</ref>

While different from the regimens of traditional sports, esports athletes still have extensive training routines. [[Team Liquid]]'s professional ''League of Legends'' team practices for a minimum of 50 hours per week and most play the game far more.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.businessinsider.com/pro-gamers-explain-the-insane-training-regimen-they-use-to-stay-on-top-2015-5|title=Here's the insane training schedule of a 20-something professional gamer|work=Business Insider|access-date=5 April 2018}}</ref> In April 2020, researchers from the [[Queensland University of Technology]] found that some of the top esports players showed similar aspects of [[mental toughness]] as [[Olympic Games|Olympic]] athletes.<ref name="QUT-20200611">{{cite news |author=[[Queensland University of Technology]] |title=Elite gamers share mental toughness with top athletes, study finds – The influence of mental toughness in elite esports |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2020-06/quot-egs061120.php |date=11 June 2020 |work=[[EurekAlert!]] |access-date=11 June 2020 }}</ref><ref name="FIP-20200423">{{cite journal |author=Poulus, Dylan |display-authors=et al. |title=Stress and Coping in Esports and the Influence of Mental Toughness |date=23 April 2020 |journal=[[Frontiers in Psychology]] |volume=11 |article-number=628 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2020.00628 |pmid=32390900 |pmc=7191198 |doi-access=free }}</ref> This training schedule for players has resulted in many of them retiring an early age. Players are generally in competition by their mid- to late-teens, with most retiring by their late-20s.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.espn.com/espn/story/_/id/13053116/esports-athletes-put-hours-training-reach-pinnacle|title=Inside an eSports training regimen|work=ESPN.com|access-date=5 April 2018}}</ref>

=== Unique players and teams ===
There is a long history of different esports teams or certain players in leagues that aren't exactly the same as most players. For example, there are many esports organizations or teams that are entirely made up of players that have [[Physical disability|physical disabilities]]. [https://www.oneesports.gg/gaming/permastunned-disabled-esports-team/ Permastunned] and [https://www.oneesports.gg/gaming/permastunned-disabled-esports-team/ ParaEsports] are great examples of this where ParaEsports is completely composed of professional ''[[Counter-Strike: Global Offensive|CS:GO]]'' players that have cerebral palsy. Whilst these teams aren't in many cases very successful in the major leagues of their respective esports, there are certain leagues or tournaments that are restricted to only have teams or players like these be able to compete. Although these teams or tournaments don't get nearly as much attention, budget, or prize pool as the main leagues of popular esports, it is still important to recognize these amazing players that have overcome their unfortunate positions and strive to succeed.

==Leagues and tournaments==
{{see also|List of esports leagues and tournaments}}

=== Promotion and relegation leagues ===
In most team-based esports, organized play is centered around the use of [[promotion and relegation]] to move sponsored teams between leagues within the competition's organization based on how the team fared in matches; this follows patterns of professional sports in European and Asian countries. Teams will play a number of games across a season as to vie for top positioning in the league by the end of that season. Those that do well, in addition to prize money, may be promoted into a higher-level league, while those that fare poorly can be regulated downward. For example, until 2018 Riot Games ran several ''League of Legends'' series, with the [[League of Legends Championship Series]] (LCS) being the top-tier series in North America and Europe. Teams that did not do well were relegated to the [[League of Legends Challenger Series]], replaced by the better performing teams from that series. This format was discontinued when Riot opted to use the franchise format in mid-2018, but has since adapted. As of 2025, the [[League of Legends Championship of The Americas]] (LTA, replacing the LCS in North America) and [[League of Legends Championship Pacific]] (LCP) have a hybrid system (first used in the [[Valorant Champions Tour]]), in which most teams are franchised and the teams that aren't can be relegated.

=== Franchised leagues ===
[[File:Fuel_vs_Excelsior_2019_Stage_3.jpg|thumb|right|A match from the second season of the Overwatch League, occurring at Blizzard Arena in Los Angeles]]
With rising interest in viewership of esports, some companies sought to create leagues that followed the franchise approach used in [[Professional sports league organization#Structure of North American leagues (Franchise and minor league system)|North American professional sports]], in which all teams, backed by a major financial sponsor to support the franchise, participate in a regular season of matches to vie for top standing as to participate in the post-season games. This approach is more attractive for larger investors, who would be more willing to back a team that remains playing in the esport's premiere league and not threatened to be relegated to a lower standing.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.chicagotribune.com/sports/breaking/ct-spt-overwatch-league-esports-espn-20180726-story.html | title = What's Overwatch? Why is it on ESPN? 8 things to know about competitive gaming | first = Jake | last = Snider | date = 26 July 2018 | access-date = 29 July 2018 | publisher = [[Associated Press]] | via=[[Chicago Tribune]] }}</ref> Though the details vary from league to league, these leagues generally require all signed player to have a minimum salary with appropriate benefits, and may share in the team's winnings. While there is no team promotion or relegation, players can be signed onto contracts, traded among teams, or let go as free agents, and new players may be pulled from the esports' equivalent [[minor league]].

The first such league to be formed was the [[Overwatch League]], established by [[Blizzard Entertainment]] in 2016 based on its ''[[Overwatch (video game)|Overwatch]]'' game.<ref name="wired">{{cite magazine | url = https://www.wired.com/story/overwatch-videogame-league-aims-to-become-new-nfl/ | title = The Overwatch Videogame League Aims to Become the New NFL | first = Nathan | last = Hill | date = 7 December 2017 | access-date = 7 December 2017 | magazine = [[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]}}</ref> Initially launched in 2018 with 12 teams, the league expanded to twenty teams in 2019. Though the first two seasons were played at [[Blizzard Arena]] in Los Angeles, the Overwatch League's third season in 2020 will implement the typical home/away game format at esports arenas in the teams' various home cities or regions.<ref name="wapost codleague" /> The OWL would fold in 2023 and would be replaced by a more open esports structure for ''Overwatch'' known as the [[Overwatch Champions Series]] (OWCS).<ref name="dotesports owl">{{cite news |last1=Esguerra |first1=Tyler |title=Blizzard confirms Overwatch League is officially dead |url=https://dotesports.com/overwatch/news/breaking-blizzard-confirms-overwatch-league-dead |access-date=8 November 2023 |work=[[Dot Esports]] |date=8 November 2023}}</ref><ref name="forbes owcs">{{cite news |last1=Gardner |first1=Matt |title='Overwatch 2' Esports Returns With All-New Champions Series For 2024 |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/mattgardner1/2024/01/23/overwatch-2-esports-returns-with-all-new-champions-series-for-2024/?sh=320f74687ffc |access-date=23 January 2024 |work=[[Forbes]] |date=23 January 2024 |language=en}}</ref>

[[Take-Two Interactive]] partnered with the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA) to create the [[NBA 2K League]], using the ''[[NBA 2K]]'' game series. It is the first esports league to be operated by a professional sports league, and the NBA sought to have a League team partially sponsored by each of the 30 professional NBA teams. Its inaugural season started in May 2018 with 17 teams and expanded up to 25 teams, including teams owned by Gen.G and Australia's [[National Basketball League (Australia)|National Basketball League]].<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/nba-take-two-to-create-professional-videogame-league-1486616461 | title = NBA, Take-Two to Create Professional Videogame League | first = Sarah | last = Needleman | date = 9 February 2017 | access-date = 14 December 2017 | work = [[The Wall Street Journal]] }}</ref><ref name="nbl oz gaming">{{cite news |title=NBL Launches NBA 2K League Team |url=https://nbl.com.au/news/nbl-launches-nba-2k-league-team |access-date=7 October 2022 |work=[[National Basketball League (Australia)|NBL]] |date=7 October 2022 |language=en}}</ref> The league entered a hiatus in 2024, returning in 2025 with a greater focus on content creators and NBA players.

Similar to the NBA 2K League, [[EA Sports]] and [[Major League Soccer]] (MLS) established the eMLS in 2018, a league using EA's ''[[FIFA (video game series)|FIFA]]'' (now known as ''[[EA Sports FC]]'') series.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2018/1/12/16880590/fifa-18-esports-world-cup-emls | title = MLS launching esports league for FIFA 18 World Cup | first = Samit | last = Sarkar | date = 12 January 2018 | access-date = 12 January 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] }}</ref> EA would later establish esports leagues with other professional football leagues, ranging from the [[Premier League|English Premier League]] to the [[Saudi Pro League]], which would feed into qualification for the [[FIFAe World Cup]] and later the EA Sports FC Pro World Championship.

[[Activision]] launched its 12-team [[Call of Duty League]] in January 2020, following the format of the Overwatch League but based on the ''[[Call of Duty]]'' series.<ref name="wapost codleague">{{cite news | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/sports/2019/09/25/new-call-duty-esports-league-will-begin-play-home-markets-start-with-teams/ |title= New Call of Duty esports league will begin play in home markets in 2020, start with 12 teams | first = Mike | last= Hume | date = 25 September 2019 | access-date = 28 September 2019 | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] }}</ref>

Cloud9 and Dignitas, among others, developed a franchise-based ''Counter-Strike: Global Offensive'' league, Flashpoint, in February 2020. This was the first such esports league to be owned by the teams rather than any single organization.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2020-02-05-team-owned-cs-go-esport-league-launched | title = Major esport organisations launch new team-owned CS:GO league | first = Haydn | last =Taylor | date = 6 February 2020 | access-date = 6 February 2020 | work = [[GamesIndustry.biz]] }}</ref> Due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] and other complications, Flashpoint would be discontinued by 2022.<ref name="Jacobwolf Flashpoint">{{cite news |last1=Wolf |first1=Jacob |title=Flashpoint dead as members walk away from competitive Counter-Strike |url=https://www.jacobwolf.report/p/flashpoint-dead-members-walk-away-competitive-counterstrike |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231203102246/https://www.jacobwolf.report/p/flashpoint-dead-members-walk-away-competitive-counterstrike |url-status=usurped |archive-date=3 December 2023 |access-date=13 February 2024 |work=The Jacob Wolf Report}}</ref>

===Tournaments===
[[File:Goście Intel Extreme Masters (8465481816).jpg|thumb|left|Casual players at the 2013 [[Intel Extreme Masters]] in [[Katowice]], Poland]]

Esports are also frequently played in tournaments, where potential players and teams vie to be placed through qualification matches before entering the tournament. From there, the tournament formats can vary from [[Single-elimination tournament|single]] or [[Double-elimination tournament|double elimination]], sometimes hybridized with [[Round-robin tournament|group stages]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gotfrag.com/portal/story/40273/ |title=GotFrag eSports – All Games News Story – TF2 Referees Wanted |publisher=Gotfrag.com |date=10 October 2007 |access-date=4 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120528203921/http://www.gotfrag.com/portal/story/40273 |archive-date=28 May 2012}}</ref> Esports tournaments are almost always physical events in which occur in front of a live audience, with referees or officials to monitor for cheating. The tournament may be part of a larger gathering, such as [[Dreamhack]], or the competition may be the entirety of the event, like the [[World Cyber Games]] or the [[Fortnite World Cup]]. Esports competitions have also become a popular feature at gaming and multi-genre [[Fan convention|conventions]].{{Citation needed|date=December 2016}}

Although competitions involving video games have long existed, esports underwent a significant transition in the late 1990s. Beginning with the [[Cyberathlete Professional League]] in 1997, tournaments became much larger, and [[sponsor (commercial)|corporate sponsorship]] became more common. Increasing viewership both in person and online brought esports to a wider audience.<ref name="2012Forbes">{{cite magazine |title=2012: The Year of eSports |magazine=Forbes |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/insertcoin/2012/12/20/2012-the-year-of-esports/ |date=20 December 2012 |first=Paul | last=Tassi |access-date=15 August 2013}}</ref><ref name="autogenerated4">{{cite web |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/2003/0808/p13s01-alsp.html?entryBottomStory |title=Are video games a sport? |publisher=CS Monitor |first=Gloria | last=Goodale |date=8 August 2003 |access-date=4 December 2013}}</ref> Major tournaments in the past included the [[World Cyber Games]], the North American [[Major League Gaming]] league, the France-based [[Electronic Sports World Cup]], and the [[World e-Sports Games]] held in [[Hangzhou]], China. The current largest esports tournament is the [[Esports World Cup]], held in Saudi Arabia as a two-month event.<ref name="Church">{{cite news |last1=Church |first1=Ben |title=Inaugural Esports World Cup in Saudi Arabia, worth more than $60M, hopes to send 'positive message' to industry |url=https://www.cnn.com/2024/04/16/sport/esports-world-cup-saudi-arabia-spt-intl/index.html |access-date=April 16, 2024 |work=[[CNN]] |date=April 16, 2024 |language=en |archive-date=June 4, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240604145817/https://www.cnn.com/2024/04/16/sport/esports-world-cup-saudi-arabia-spt-intl/index.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Traditional sports teams earn revenue from ticket sales, media rights, advertising, and sponsorships, whereas e‑sports teams depend largely on tournament prize money, sponsorships, and advertising.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=Young Hoon |last2=Nauright |first2=John |last3=Suveatwatanakul |first3=Chokechai |date=2020-11-01 |title=The rise of E-Sports and potential for Post-COVID continued growth |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17430437.2020.1819695 |journal=Sport in Society |language=en |volume=23 |issue=11 |pages=1861–1871 |doi=10.1080/17430437.2020.1819695 |issn=1743-0437|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The average compensation for professional esports players does not compare to those of the top classical sports organizations in the world. According to Julian Krinsky Camps & Programs website, the top Esports player in the world earned around $2.5 million in 2017.<ref name=":0">{{cite web | publisher=Julian Krinsky Camps and Programs | date=5 June 2018 | title=How Much Do Pro Gamers & Esports Players Make? | access-date=29 April 2020 | url=https://info.jkcp.com/blog/professional-gamer-salary-esports/ | archive-date=8 April 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200408051135/https://info.jkcp.com/blog/professional-gamer-salary-esports/ }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Top Players of 2017 - History :: Esports Earnings |url=https://www.esportsearnings.com/history/2017/top_players |access-date=2026-02-18 |website=www.esportsearnings.com}}</ref> The highest overall salary by any esports professional at the time was around $3.6 million. While prizes for esports competitions can be very large, the limited number of competitions and large number of competitors ultimately lowers the amount of money one can make in the industry. The most prestigious esports competitions have prizes that can reach or exceed $200,000 for a single victory; Dota 2's [[The International (esports)|The International]] hosted a competition where the grand-prize winning team walked home with almost $10.9 million.<ref name=":0" />

For well established games, total prize money can amount to millions of U.S. dollars a year.<ref name="lolprizepool" /><ref>{{cite web |url=http://archive.esfiworld.com/news/nasl-s3-finals-push-sc2-earnings-over-5m |title=NASL S3 Finals push SC2 earnings over $5m |first=David | last=Schmidt |date=16 July 2012 |publisher=ESFI World |access-date=22 August 2012 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212160245/http://archive.esfiworld.com/news/nasl-s3-finals-push-sc2-earnings-over-5m |archive-date=12 December 2013}}</ref> As of 10 September 2016, ''Dota 2'' has awarded approximately US$86 million in prize money within 632 registered tournaments, with 23 players winning over $1 million. ''League of Legends'' awarded approximately $30 million within 1749 registered tournaments, but in addition to the prize money, [[Riot Games]] provides salaries for players within their professional leagues.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://gamurs.com/articles/comparing-the-potential-earnings-of-lcs-players-to-professional-streamers |title=Comparing the potential earnings of LCS PLayers to Professional Streamers |website=GAMURS |date=27 October 2014 |access-date=4 July 2016 |archive-date=6 October 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161006061500/https://gamurs.com/articles/comparing-the-potential-earnings-of-lcs-players-to-professional-streamers }}</ref> Nonetheless, there has been criticism to how these salaries are distributed, since most players earn a fairly low wage but a few top players have a significantly higher salary, skewing the average earning per player.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://krbnu.tumblr.com/post/135814946168/kespa-responds-to-kocca-pro-gamer-salary-data-10 |title=KeSPA Responds to KOCCA Pro Gamer Salary Data… 10 Players Over $85,241. |website=LCK Translation Archive |date=24 December 2015 |access-date=10 September 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160406101703/http://krbnu.tumblr.com/post/135814946168/kespa-responds-to-kocca-pro-gamer-salary-data-10 |archive-date=6 April 2016 }}</ref> In August 2018, [[The International 2018]], Valve's annual premier ''Dota 2'' tournament, was held and broke the record for holding the largest prize pool to date for any esports tournament, amounting to over US$25 million.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 2017–2018 Dota 2 Hub |url=http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/18749881/the-dota-2-espn-esports-homepage |website=ESPN |date=26 August 2018 |access-date=31 January 2019}}</ref>

Often, game developers provide prize money for tournament competition directly,<ref name="lolprizepool">{{cite web |url=http://pc.ign.com/articles/122/1224149p1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120508094235/http://pc.ign.com/articles/122/1224149p1.html |archive-date=8 May 2012 |title=League of Legends Season 2 Championship Announced |first=Andrew | last=Goldfarb |date=1 May 2012 |website=IGN |access-date=22 August 2012}}</ref> but sponsorship may also come from third parties, typically companies selling [[computer hardware]], [[energy drink]]s, or [[computer software]]. Generally, hosting a large esports event is not profitable as a stand-alone venture.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.theverge.com/2013/9/30/4719766/twitch-raises-20-million-esports-market-booming |title=Field of streams: how Twitch made video games a spectator sport |publisher=TheVerge |first=Ben | last=Popper |date=30 September 2013 |access-date=4 December 2013}}</ref> For example, Riot has stated that their headline ''League of Legends'' Championship Series is "a significant investment that we're not making money from".<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pcgamesn.com/leagueoflegends/lcs-significant-investment-we-re-not-making-money-riot-love-it-anyway |title=LCS "a significant investment that we're not making money from", but Riot love it anyway |publisher=PCGamesN |author=robzacny |date=21 August 2013 |access-date=14 September 2013}}</ref>

There is considerable variation and negotiation over the relationship between [[video game developers]] and tournament organizers and broadcasters. While the original ''StarCraft'' events emerged in South Korea largely independently of Blizzard, the company decided to require organizers and broadcasters to authorize events featuring the sequel ''StarCraft II''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.edge-online.com/features/battle-starcraft-ii/ |publisher=Edge-Online |title=The battle for StarCraft II |date=11 November 2010 |author=Edge Staff |access-date=14 September 2013}}</ref> In the short term, this led to a deadlock with the [[Korean e-Sports Association]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gosugamers.net/starcraft/news/10265-blizzard-vs-kespa-the-ultimate-fight |title=Blizzard VS. Kespa, the Ultimate fight |author=Simon "Go0g3n" |publisher=Gosu Gamers |year=2009 |access-date=18 September 2013}}</ref> An agreement was reached in 2012.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://pikigeek.com/2012/05/02/kespa-ogn-blizzard-and-gomtv-join-horses-for-starcraft-ii/ |title=KeSPA, OGN, Blizzard and GOMtv Join Horses for StarCraft II |publisher=PikiGeek |date=2 May 2012 |author=Jeroen Amin |access-date=14 September 2013 |archive-date=7 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171107110126/http://pikigeek.com/2012/05/02/kespa-ogn-blizzard-and-gomtv-join-horses-for-starcraft-ii/ }}</ref> Blizzard requires authorization for tournaments with more than US$10,000 in prizes.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bnetcmsus-a.akamaihd.net/cms/gallery/4RL7ZGLM5EF21374101567640.pdf |title=Tournament Guidelines Document |publisher=Blizzard |date=6 June 2013 |access-date=14 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131231001601/https://bnetcmsus-a.akamaihd.net/cms/gallery/4RL7ZGLM5EF21374101567640.pdf |archive-date=31 December 2013 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Riot Games]] offers in-game rewards to authorized tournaments.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://na.leagueoflegends.com/en/community/prized-events |title=Prized Events |publisher=Riot |access-date=4 December 2013 |archive-date=13 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150713191712/http://na.leagueoflegends.com/en/community/prized-events }}</ref>

===University and school leagues===
{{See also|College esports in the United States}}

The increasing popularity of esports brought with it a demand for extended opportunities for esports athletes. Esports clubs grew in popularity at American universities in the late 2000s and early 2010s, with ''[[StarCraft]]'' clubs competing by 2009.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Cohen |first1=Patricia |title=Video Game Becomes Spectator Sport |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/04/12/sports/othersports/12star.html |website=New York Times |date=12 April 2009 |access-date=30 September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Princeton Students Create StarCraft League |url=https://www.escapistmagazine.com/princeton-students-create-starcraft-league/ |website=The Escapist |access-date=30 September 2024 |date=14 April 2009}}</ref> Universities, particularly in China and America, then began offering scholarship opportunities to incoming students to join collegiate esports teams. The first officially recognized varsity esports program was created at [[Robert Morris University]] in 2014.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Keilman |first1=John |title=Robert Morris' video gamers enter 1st competition |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2014/10/19/robert-morris-video-gamers-enter-1st-competition/ |website=Chicago Tribune |access-date=30 September 2024 |date=19 October 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Brunswick |first1=Deborah |title=Varsity gamers: Making history and dumbfounding parents |url=https://www.cnn.com/interactive/2015/07/us/varsity-gamers-american-story/ |website=CNN.com |access-date=30 September 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Gamers to get college scholarships |url=https://www.espn.com/chicago/college-sports/story/_/id/11113637/robert-morris-university-offers-esports-scholarships-league-legends-video-game |website=ESPN.com |access-date=30 September 2024 |language=en |date=20 June 2014}}</ref> {{As of |2019|post=,}} around 125 US colleges had esports-based varsity programs. Most of these are members of the National Association of Collegiate Esports.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.espn.com/esports/story/_/id/21152905/college-esports-list-varsity-esports-programs-north-america|title=List of varsity esports programs spans North America|work=ESPN.com|access-date=31 January 2020|language=en}}</ref>

The UK's National University Esports League (NUEL) started in 2010. In 2023, it was taken over by Spanish Esports company GGTech Entertainment.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://esportsinsider.com/2023/05/nuel-acquired-by-ggtech-entertainment|title=University esports company NUEL acquired by GGTech|author=Ivan Šimić |date=24 May 2023|work=Esports Insider}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://esports-news.co.uk/2023/08/09/nuel-ggtech-interview-david-josh/|title=UK University Esports: Interview with NUEL and GGTech at Amazon University Esports Masters Finals|date=9 August 2023| author=Dom Sacco|work=Esports News UK}}</ref> {{As of|2024|post=,}} it had been rebranded as [[University Esports]] UK & Ireland and had over 110 participating universities.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://universityesports.co.uk/about-us|title=About us|website=University Esports UK & Ireland|access-date=27 September 2024}}</ref> Another university competition in the UK is the British Universities Esports Championship, run by National Student Esports (NSE), which also had over 110 participating universities and colleges {{As of|2024|lc=y}}. The University of Warwick won its sixth consecutive NES Esports University of the Year title in 2024.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.nse.gg/news/esports-university-of-the-year-20232024/|title=Esports University of the Year 2023/2024|date=10 April 2024|website=National Student Esports}}</ref> The two organisations are not exclusive, with universities able to field teams in both NUEL and NSE competitions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.durham.ac.uk/colleges-and-student-experience/enrichment-activities/esports/|title=eSports at Durham|access-date=27 September 2024|website=Durham University}}</ref> For younger students, the British Esports Student Champs had over 1,250 teams from over 200 schools and colleges {{As of|2024|lc=y}}.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://britishesports.org/student-champs/#openreg|title=The Student Champs|website=British Esports Federation|access-date=25 September 2024}}</ref> Collegiate universities such as Durham and multi-campus universities such as Staffordshire also hold inter-collegiate or inter-campus tournaments.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://esports-news.co.uk/2024/09/28/durham-university-opens-esports-hub/|title=Durham University opens new esports hub|date=28 September 2024|author= Dom Sacco|work=Esports News UK}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://esports-news.co.uk/2024/05/18/staffs-uni-campus-clash-facilities/|title=Staffs Uni hosts Campus Clash as new £2.7m esports facilities open|date=18 May 2024|author= Dom Sacco|work=Esports News UK}}</ref>

According to Schaeperkoetter and collaborators in 2017, the potential impact of esports programs on universities, coupled with the growing interest that universities were showing in such programs, combined to make esports a relevant line of research in sport literature.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1123/jis.2016-0011|title=The "New" Student-Athlete: An Exploratory Examination of Scholarship e ''Sports'' Players|year=2017|last1=Schaeperkoetter|first1=Claire C.|last2=Mays|first2=Jonathan|last3=Hyland|first3=Sean Thomas|last4=Wilkerson|first4=Zach|last5=Oja|first5=Brent|last6=Krueger|first6=Kyle|last7=Christian|first7=Ronald|last8=Bass|first8=Jordan R.|journal=Journal of Intercollegiate Sport|volume=10|pages=1–21|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Governing bodies===

While game publishers or esports broadcasters typically act in oversight roles for specific esports, a number of esports [[sport governing body|governing bodies]] have been established to collectively represent esports on a national, regional or global basis. These governing bodies may have various levels of involvement with the esport, from being part of esports regulation to simply acting more as a [[trade group]] and public face for esports.

The [[International Esports Federation]] (IESF) was one of the first such bodies. Originally formed in 2008 to help promote esports in the Southeast Asian region, it has grown to include over 140 member countries from across the globe. The IESF has managed annual World Esports Championships for teams from its member countries across multiple games.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.insidethegames.biz/articles/1076046/seoul-to-host-2019-esports-world-championships | title = Seoul to host 2019 Esports World Championships | first = Mike | last = Rowbottom | date = 28 February 2019 | access-date = 20 December 2019 | work = [[Inside the Games]] }}</ref>

The European Esports Federation was formed in April 2019 and includes UK, Belgium, Germany, Austria, Hungary, France, Russia, Slovenia, Serbia, Sweden, Turkey, and Ukraine. This body was designed more to be a managing partner for other esports, working to coordinate event structures and regulations across multiple esports.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://esportsobserver.com/european-esports-federation-formed/ | title = European Esports Federation to Form With 12 National Members | first = Graham | last = Ashton | date= 18 April 2019 | access-date = 20 December 2019 | work = [[The Esports Observer]] }}</ref>

Additionally, trade groups representing video games have also generally acted as governing bodies for esports. Notably, in November 2019, five major national trade organizations – the [[Entertainment Software Association]] in the United States, the [[Entertainment Software Association of Canada]], [[The Association for UK Interactive Entertainment]], Interactive Software Federation of Europe, and the [[Interactive Games and Entertainment Association]] of Australian and New Zealand – issued a joined statement for supporting the promotion and participation of esports to respect player safety and integrity, respect and diversity among players, and enriching game play.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2019-11-05-games-industry-international-trade-bodies-unite-on-universal-esports-principles | title = Games industry international trade bodies unite on universal esports principles | first= Rebekah | last = Valentine | date = 5 November 2019 | access-date= 20 December 2019 | work = [[GamesIndustry.biz]] }}</ref>

==Criticisms and legal problems==

=== Health concerns ===
{{See also|Video game addiction|Video game–related health problems}}

Most esports generally require participants to sit and/or move little while playing, which raises concerns about a [[sedentary lifestyle]] by players. A research led by Ingo Froböse, a professor at the [[German Sport University Cologne|German Sports University in Cologne]], for over eight years found professional and also amateur esports gamers play on average 24–25 hours per week and even physical activities after hours of playing are not able to compensate the damage of oversitting. Players in China may train for almost 14 hours a day. A study conducted in 2022 of ''CS:GO'' players found that total hours played were about 31.2 hours each week.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pluss |first1=Matthew A. |last2=Novak |first2=Andrew R. |last3=Bennett |first3=Kyle J. M. |last4=McBride |first4=Ignatius |last5=Panchuk |first5=Derek |last6=Coutts |first6=Aaron J. |last7=Fransen |first7=Job |date=1 December 2022 |title=Examining the game-specific practice behaviors of professional and semi-professional esports players: A 52-week longitudinal study |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563222002436 |journal=Computers in Human Behavior |language=en |volume=137 |article-number=107421 |doi=10.1016/j.chb.2022.107421 |s2cid=251260420 |issn=0747-5632|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Sitting for long periods at a computer could lead to eye [[fatigue]] and lower back pain from poor posture. Gamers with poor posture sit in [[forward head posture]] which can cause symptoms such as decreased arm or shoulder mobility and tension headaches.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Migliore |first1=Lindsey |title=Neck and Back Disorders in Esports |date=2021 |work=Handbook of Esports Medicine: Clinical Aspects of Competitive Video Gaming |pages=71–118 |editor-last=Migliore |editor-first=Lindsey |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-73610-1_3 |isbn=978-3-030-73610-1 |last2=McGee |first2=Caitlin |s2cid=236650862 |editor2-last=McGee |editor2-first=Caitlin |editor3-last=Moore |editor3-first=Melita N.}}</ref> These [[sedentary behavior]]s of sitting for too long concerns public health researchers because spending more than 6–8 hours per day has been linked to increased risk of [[cardiovascular disease]] and all-cause mortality.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Patterson |first1=Richard |last2=McNamara |first2=Eoin |last3=Tainio |first3=Marko |last4=de Sá |first4=Thiago Hérick |last5=Smith |first5=Andrea D. |last6=Sharp |first6=Stephen J. |last7=Edwards |first7=Phil |last8=Woodcock |first8=James |last9=Brage |first9=Søren |last10=Wijndaele |first10=Katrien |date=September 2018 |title=Sedentary behaviour and risk of all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality, and incident type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and dose response meta-analysis |journal=European Journal of Epidemiology |language=en |volume=33 |issue=9 |pages=811–829 |doi=10.1007/s10654-018-0380-1 |pmid=29589226 |pmc=6133005 |issn=0393-2990}}</ref> As a result, teams like [[T1 (esports)|T1]] have partnered with [[Nike, Inc.|Nike]] to encourage exercise and provide training that helps improve gaming skills.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hao |first=Dexter Tan Guan |date=16 January 2020 |title=T1 signs global partnership with Nike |url=https://dotesports.com/news/t1-signs-global-partnership-with-nike |access-date=15 February 2023 |website=Dot Esports |language=en-US}}</ref> Recent research has also shown that structured esports activities can foster teamwork, problem-solving skills, and promote digital literacy among participants, though concerns about sedentary behavior and mental health risks persist.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Choi |first1=Wonjun |last2=Jang |first2=Wooyoung (William) |last3=Song |first3=Hyunseok |last4=Kim |first4=Min Jung |last5=Lee |first5=Wonju |last6=Byon |first6=Kevin K. |date=9 July 2024 |title=Esports for development? Exploring esports player profiles and their development and well-being outcomes |url=https://www.emerald.com/insight/content/doi/10.1108/IJSMS-08-2023-0160/full/html |journal=International Journal of Sports Marketing and Sponsorship |language=en |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=684–704 |doi=10.1108/IJSMS-08-2023-0160 |issn=1464-6668|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In addition to sedentary behaviors, players' mental health is a concern for scientists. One study found that competitors in esports are often under psychological and physical stress, and the amateur ones are the most affected, since they frequently aim at greater wins without enough preparation, though no clear training guidelines are set to become professional players.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Are esports good for your health? – DW – 02/08/2019 |url=https://www.dw.com/en/are-esports-good-for-your-health/a-47408527 |access-date=19 January 2023 |website=dw.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=eSportwissen.de |last2=Tholl |first2=Chuck |date=21 June 2018 |title=[:de]Leistung im eSport[:en]Performance in eSport[:] |url=https://www.esportwissen.de/en/performance-in-esport/ |access-date=19 January 2023 |website=esportwissen.de |language=en-US}}</ref> Researchers have found that high levels of stress lead to mental illness and poor decision making.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wattanapisit |first1=Apichai |last2=Wattanapisit |first2=Sanhapan |last3=Wongsiri |first3=Sunton |date=May 2020 |title=Public Health Perspectives on eSports |journal=Public Health Reports |language=en |volume=135 |issue=3 |pages=295–298 |doi=10.1177/0033354920912718 |issn=0033-3549 |pmc=7238713 |pmid=32237971}}</ref> The Esports sector has a high rate of burnout due to mental health and stress. A study found a correlation between depression and training time leading to sleep disturbances.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Sangha |last2=Bonnar |first2=Daniel |last3=Roane |first3=Brandy |last4=Gradisar |first4=Michael |last5=Dunican |first5=Ian C. |last6=Lastella |first6=Michele |last7=Maisey |first7=Gemma |last8=Suh |first8=Sooyeon |date=January 2021 |title=Sleep Characteristics and Mood of Professional Esports Athletes: A Multi-National Study |journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health |language=en |volume=18 |issue=2 |page=664 |doi=10.3390/ijerph18020664 |pmid=33466788 |pmc=7830734 |issn=1660-4601 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Teams are starting to incorporate mental health support for players. For example, the organization [[Misfits Gaming]] has hired a psychologist to ensure players are equipped with methods to deal with stress and anxiety.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Stubbs |first=Mike |title=Why Esports Team Misfits Is Prioritizing Mental Health For Players And Staff |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/mikestubbs/2021/06/09/why-esports-team-misfits-is-prioritizing-mental-health-for-players-and-staff/ |access-date=15 February 2023 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref>

===Ethical issues===
Esports athletes are usually obligated to behave ethically, abiding by both the explicit rules set out by tournaments, associations, and teams, as well as following general expectations of good [[sportsmanship]]. For example, it is common practice and considered good etiquette to send a "gg" (good game) message to opponents when defeated.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.techhive.com/article/248526/web_jargon_origins_revealed.html |title=Web Jargon Origins Revealed |author=David Daw |work=TechHive |date=21 January 2012 |access-date=22 September 2013 |archive-date=15 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151015235725/http://www.techhive.com/article/248526/web_jargon_origins_revealed.html }}</ref> Many games rely on competitors having limited information about the game state. In a prominent example of good conduct, during a 2012 [[Intel Extreme Masters|IEM]] ''StarCraft II'' game, players Feast and DeMusliM voluntarily offered information about their strategies to negate the influence of outside information inadvertently leaked to Feast during the game.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cadred.org/News/Article/167534/ |title=IEM Sao Paolo: Manner Bear Conflict |publisher=Cadred |author=Victor Meulendijks |date=8 February 2012 |access-date=8 October 2013 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20131008224558/http://www.cadred.org/News/Article/167534/ |archive-date=8 October 2013 }}</ref> Players in some leagues have been reprimanded for failing to meet expectations of good behavior. In 2012, professional ''League of Legends'' player Christian "IWillDominate" Riviera was banned from competing for one year following a history of verbal abuse.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://forums.na.leagueoflegends.com/board/showthread.php?t=2864421 |title=IWillDominate Tribunal Permaban & eSports Competition Ruling |date=4 December 2012 |access-date=9 November 2014 |archive-date=26 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171026045406/http://forums.na.leagueoflegends.com/board/showthread.php?t=2864421 }}</ref> In 2013, ''StarCraft II'' progamer [[Greg "Idra" Fields]] was fired from [[Evil Geniuses]] for insulting his fans on the [[Team Liquid]] internet forums.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.teamliquid.net/forum/viewmessage.php?topic_id=411840 |title=Evil Geniuses Releases Greg "IdrA" Fields |author=Alexander Garfield |publisher=TeamLiquid |date=10 May 2013 |access-date=8 January 2014}}</ref> ''League of Legends'' players Mithy and Nukeduck received similar penalties in 2014 after behaving in a "toxic" manner during matches.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/league-of-legends-pro-players-banned-for-toxic-behavior/1100-6420072/ |title=League of Legends Pro Players Banned for "Toxic Behavior" |date=3 June 2014 |access-date=22 February 2015}}</ref>

There have been serious rule violations in certain esports. In 2010, eleven ''StarCraft: Brood War'' players were found guilty of [[StarCraft professional competition#Match fixing scandal|fixing matches for profit]] and were fined and banned from future competition. [[Team Curse]] and [[Team Dignitas]] were denied prize money for collusion during the [[2012 MLG Summer Championship]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pcgamesn.com/leagueoflegends/league-legends-curse-na-and-team-dignitas-disqualified-mlg-summer-championship-no-first-or-second-place-awarded |title=League of Legends' Curse NA and Team Dignitas disqualified from MLG Summer Championship, no first or second place awarded |author=Jeremy Peel |publisher=PC GamesN |date=27 August 2012 |access-date=22 September 2013}}</ref> In 2012, ''League of Legends'' team Azubu Frost was fined US$30,000 for cheating during a semifinal match of the world playoffs.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/news/riot-fines-league-of-legends-cheaters-30000-6398055 |title=Riot fines League of Legends cheaters $30,000 |author=Laura Parker |website=GameSpot |date=10 October 2012 |access-date=22 September 2013}}</ref> ''Dota 2'' player Aleksey "Solo" Berezin was suspended from several tournaments for intentionally throwing a game to collect $322 from online gambling.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.joindota.com/en/news/10165-solo-out-of-rox-kis |title=Solo out of Rox.KIS |author=Sun_tzu |publisher=joinDota |date=21 June 2013 |access-date=3 July 2014}}</ref> In 2014, four high-profile North American ''Counter-Strike'' players from iBuyPower were suspended from official tournaments after being found guilty of match-fixing, allegedly profiting over US$10,000 through betting on their fixed matches.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/articles/valve-bans-pro-counter-strike-teams-for-match-fixi/1100-6424901/ |title=Valve Bans Pro Counter-Strike Teams For Match Fixing |work=GameSpot |access-date=2 September 2015}}</ref>

[[Skin gambling|Gambling on esports using ''Counter-Strike: Global Offensive'' "skins"]], worth an estimated US$2.3 billion in 2015, came under criticism in June and July 2016 after several questionable legal and ethical aspects were discovered.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-36824689 |title=Valve tackles Counter Strike gambling sites |work=[[BBC]] |date=21 July 2016 |access-date=21 July 2016}}</ref>

===Performance-enhancing drugs===
{{main|Cheating in esports#Doping}}

Reports of widespread use of [[performance-enhancing drugs]] (PEDs) in esports are not uncommon, with players discussing their own, their teammates' and their competitors' use as well as officials acknowledging the prevalence of the issue.<ref name="parkin">{{cite web |last1=Parkin |first1=Simon |title=Winners might use drugs |url=http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2015-04-08-winners-might-use-drugs |access-date=19 July 2015 |website=[[Eurogamer]] |date=8 April 2015}}</ref><ref name="newscientist">{{cite magazine |last1=Hodson |first1=Hal |title=Esports: Doping is rampant, industry insider claims |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn26051-esports-doping-is-rampant-industry-insider-claims#.U-x3KvldU0J |access-date=19 July 2015 |magazine=[[New Scientist]] |date=18 August 2014}}</ref><ref name="summers">{{cite web |last1=Summers |first1=Nick |title=Top 'Counter-Strike' player admits eSports has a doping problem |url=https://www.engadget.com/2015/07/17/esports-adderall-doping/ |access-date=19 July 2015 |publisher=[[Engadget]] |date=17 July 2015}}</ref> Players often turn to [[stimulants]] such as [[Ritalin]], [[Adderall]] and [[Vyvanse]], drugs which can significantly boost concentration, improve reaction time, and prevent fatigue.<ref name="parkin" /> [[Selegiline]], a drug used to treat [[Parkinson's disease]], is reportedly popular, because like stimulants, it enhances mood and motivation. Conversely, drugs with calming effects are also sought after. Some players take [[propranolol]], which blocks the effects of [[adrenaline]], or [[Valium]], which is prescribed to treat [[anxiety disorder]], in order to remain calm under pressure.<ref name="newscientist" /> According to Bjoern Franzen, a former [[SK Gaming]] executive, it is second nature for some ''League of Legends'' players to take as many as three different drugs before competition.<ref name="elephant">{{cite web |last1=Franzen |first1=Bjoern |title=Doping in eSports – The almost invisible Elephant in the room |url=https://bjoernfranzen.com/doping-in-esports-the-almost-invisible-elephant-in-the-room/ |access-date=19 July 2015 |work=BjoernFranzen.com |date=14 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210422153147/https://bjoernfranzen.com/doping-in-esports-the-almost-invisible-elephant-in-the-room/ |archive-date=22 April 2021 |url-status=live}}</ref> In July 2015 Kory "Semphis" Friesen, an ex-[[Cloud9 (esports)|Cloud9]] player, admitted that he and his teammates were all using Adderall during a match against [[Virtus.pro]] in the [[ESL One Katowice 2015]] ''Counter-Strike: Global Offensive'' tournament, and went on to claim that "everyone" at [[ESEA League]] tournaments uses Adderall.<ref name="summers" /> In 2020, former Call of Duty champion Adam "KiLLa" Sloss told [[The Washington Post]] that one of the major reasons he stopped competing in esports was the "rampant" use of Adderall in the competitive scene.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hamstead |first1=Coleman |title='Nobody talks about it because everyone is on it': Adderall presents esports with an enigma |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/esports/2020/02/13/esports-adderall-drugs/ |newspaper=Washington Post |access-date=23 September 2021 |date=13 February 2021}}</ref>

The unregulated use of such drugs poses severe risks to competitors' health, including [[addiction]], [[overdose]], [[serotonin syndrome]] and, in the case of stimulants, [[weight loss]].<ref name=parkin /><ref name="newscientist" /> Accordingly, Adderall and other such stimulants are banned and their use penalized by many professional sporting bodies and leagues, including [[Major League Baseball]] and the [[National Football League]]. Although [[International e-Sports Federation]] (IeSF) is a signatory of the [[World Anti-Doping Agency]], the governing body has not outlawed any PEDs in its sanctioned competitions.<ref name="parkin" /> Action has been taken on the individual league level, however, as at least one major league, the [[Electronic Sports League]], has made use of any drugs during matches punishable by expulsion from competition.<ref>{{cite web |title=ESL Major Series One Rulebook |url=http://gfx.esl-europe.net/gfx/media/eu/emsone/summer2013/ESL_Major_Series_One_Rulebook.pdf |publisher=[[Electronic Sports League]] |access-date=19 July 2015 |archive-date=22 July 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150722105358/http://gfx.esl-europe.net/gfx/media/eu/emsone/summer2013/ESL_Major_Series_One_Rulebook.pdf }}</ref> Although not all players use drugs, the use of over-the-counter [[energy drinks]] is common. These energy drinks are often marketed specifically toward gamers, and have also faced media and regulatory scrutiny due to their health risks.<ref name="fuel">{{cite web |last1=Stout |first1=Hilary |title=Selling the Young on 'Gaming Fuel' |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/05/20/business/energy-drink-industry-under-scrutiny-looks-to-gamers-to-keep-sales-surging.html |access-date=19 July 2015 |work=The New York Times |date=19 May 2015}}</ref>

===Player exploitation===
There has been some concern over the quality of life and potential mistreatment of players by organizations, especially in South Korea. Korean organizations have been accused of refusing to pay competitive salaries, leading to a slow exodus of Korean players to other markets. In an interview, ''League of Legends'' player Bae "Dade" Eo-jin said that "Korean players wake up at 1 pm and play until 5 am", and suggested that the 16-hour play schedule was a significant factor in causing [[Burnout (psychology)|burnout]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://na.lolesports.com/articles/koreas-pro-exodus-may-spell-bad-news-games-top-region |title=KOREA'S PRO EXODUS MAY SPELL BAD NEWS FOR THE GAME'S TOP REGION |publisher=Riot Games |author=Frank 'Riot Mirhi' Fields |date=5 November 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref> Concerns over the [[mental health]] of players intensified in 2014 when ''League of Legends'' player Cheon "Promise" Min-Ki attempted suicide a week after admitting to [[match fixing]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.polygon.com/2014/3/18/5522192/korean-league-of-legends-player-fixed-matches-suicide |title=Top Korean League of Legends player fixed matches before attempting suicide, says eSports league |website=Polygon |author=Owen S. Good |date=18 March 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014}}</ref>

To combat the negative environment, Korean ''League of Legends'' teams were given new rules for the upcoming 2015 season by Riot Games, including the adoption of minimum salaries for professional players, requiring contracts and allowing players to stream individually for additional player revenue.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ongamers.com/articles/major-changes-heading-to-korea-for-the-2015-season/1100-2303/ |title=Major changes heading to Korea for the 2015 season |publisher=OnGamers |author=Travis Gafford |date=27 October 2014 |access-date=9 November 2014 |archive-date=10 December 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151210201355/http://www.ongamers.com/articles/major-changes-heading-to-korea-for-the-2015-season/1100-2303/ }}</ref>

Since esports games often requires many actions per minute, some players may get [[repetitive strain]] injuries, causing hand or wrist pain.<ref>Luke Winkie (31 May 2016) [http://www.vocativ.com/323427/the-esports-injury-crisis/ The eSports Injury Crisis] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180110040656/http://www.vocativ.com/323427/the-esports-injury-crisis/ |date=10 January 2018 }} Vocativ, Retrieved 3 June 2016.</ref> During the early development of the esports industry, sports medicine and gaming-related injuries were ignored by players and organizations, leading to some early player retirements.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Leporati |first1=Gregory |title=Aching wrists, early retirement and the surprising physical toll of esports |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/esports/2022/03/14/professional-esports-athlete-injuries/ |newspaper=Washington Post |access-date=21 March 2022}}</ref>

=== Women ===
{{See also|Women and video games}}
The number of female viewers has been growing in esports, with an estimated 30% of esports viewers being female in 2013, a significant increase from 15% the previous year.{{Citation needed|date=January 2017}} However, despite the increase in female viewers, there are still very few female players in high level competitive esports.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kordyaka |first=Bastian |last2=Pumplun |first2=Luisa |last3=Brunnhofer |first3=Marlies |last4=Kruse |first4=Bjoern |last5=Laato |first5=Samuli |date=2023-12-01 |title=Gender disparities in esports – An explanatory mixed-methods approach |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563223003072 |journal=Computers in Human Behavior |volume=149 |article-number=107956 |doi=10.1016/j.chb.2023.107956 |issn=0747-5632|doi-access=free }}</ref> As of 2024, 33% of European e-sports viewers are female.<ref>{{Cite web |date=Dec 2024 |title=Let's Play! 2024: The esports market |url=https://www.deloitte.com/content/dam/assets-zone2/de/de/docs/industries/technology-media-telecommunications/2024/Deloitte-Lets-Play-Esports-final-%202024.pdf |access-date=1 Jan 2026 |website=Deloitte}}</ref> The top female players that are involved in esports mainly get exposure in female-only tournaments, most notably ''Counter-Strike'', ''[[Dead or Alive 4]]'', and ''StarCraft II''. Current all-female esports teams include [[Frag Dolls]] and [[PMS Clan]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2017}}

The formation of Team Siren, an all-female ''[[League of Legends]]'' team, in June 2013 was met with controversy and dismissed as a "gimmick" to attract men's attention.<ref>{{cite web |date=30 May 2013 |title=Introducing Team Siren – YouTube |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_Gz9um3wV1o |website=[[YouTube]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=10 June 2013 |title=Why Team Siren Matters |url=http://www.rtsguru.com/game/435/article/5991/Why-Team-Siren-Matters.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924092521/http://www.rtsguru.com/game/435/article/5991/Why-Team-Siren-Matters.html |archive-date=24 September 2015 |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref> The team disbanded within a month due to negative publicity from their promotional video and the team captain's poor attitude towards her teammates.<ref>{{cite web |date=19 June 2013 |title=Siren broke up (with proof) – Page 16 – League of Legends Community |url=http://forums.na.leagueoflegends.com/board/showthread.php?p=38929204#post38929204 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170311162545/http://forums.na.leagueoflegends.com/board/showthread.php?p=38929204#post38929204 |archive-date=11 March 2017 |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=26 June 2013 |title=League of Legends Team Siren Disbands: Valuable Lessons Learned – League of Legends |url=http://www.gameskinny.com/hzi5j/league-of-legends-team-siren-disbands-valuable-lessons-learned |access-date=27 December 2014}}</ref> In 2018, [[Vaevictis Esports|Team Vaevictis]] attempted to field an all-female roster in the [[League of Legends Continental League|LCL]], the top esports league in Russia,<ref>{{cite tweet |number=1094686736570032132 |user=VaevictisTeam |title=We're proud to present you Vaevictis eSports roster for LCL Spring 2019! |author=Vaevictis eSports |date=10 February 2019 |access-date=3 June 2019}}</ref> but faced similar criticism.<ref>{{cite news |date=17 February 2019 |title=All-female Russian LoL team Vaevictis Esports lose 52–2 in the LCL: Is this really about giving women a platform or is it just an unfair publicity stunt? |url=https://esports-news.co.uk/2019/02/17/vaevictis-esports-all-female-team/ |access-date=3 June 2019 |work=Esports News UK}}</ref> Vaevictis went 0–14 in both splits, and in February 2020, the LCL announced their disbandment due to a failure to field a competitive roster.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 February 2020 |title=League of Legends: Vaevictis eSports removed from LCL due to poor results |url=https://www.millenium.gg/news/12786.html |access-date=25 November 2020 |website=Millenium US |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Vaevictis female roster removed from LCL |url=https://www.earlygame.com/vaevictis-female-roster-experiment-ends-in-expulsion-from-lcl/ |access-date=25 November 2020 |website=EarlyGame |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=17 February 2020 |title=League of Legends: All-female team Vaevictis kicked out of LCL due to poor performance; CrowCrowd, owned by former player Likkrit joins the league |url=https://www.invenglobal.com/articles/10417/all-female-team-vaevictis-kicked-out-of-lcl-due-to-poor-performance-crowcrowd-owned-by-former-player-likkrit-joins-the-league |access-date=25 November 2020 |website=InvenGlobal |language=en}}</ref> The LCL stated, "The results of the 2019 season showed a huge difference in Vaevictis Esports' results compared to other LCL teams, which is an unacceptable level of competitiveness in a franchised league."

===Economics===
The [[League of Legends Championship Series|''League of Legends'' Championship Series]] and [[League of Legends Champions Korea|''League of Legends'' Champions Korea]] offer guaranteed [[salaries]] for players.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newsoflegends.com/index.php/official-2015-season-lol-esports-league-reform-plan-announced-final-version-29648/ |title=Official 2015 Season LoL eSports League Reform Plan Announced (Final Version) |website=News of Legends |date=11 November 2014 |author=Caymus |access-date=28 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518084152/http://www.newsoflegends.com/index.php/official-2015-season-lol-esports-league-reform-plan-announced-final-version-29648/ |archive-date=18 May 2015 }}</ref> Despite this, online streaming is preferred by some players, as in some cases, streaming can be more profitable than competing with a team, and streamers have the ability to determine their own schedule. The International tournament awards US$10 million to the winners, however teams that do not have the same amount of success often do not have financial stability and frequently break up after failing to win.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.dailydot.com/esports/dota-2-prize-distribution-players/ |title=Dota 2 is the richest of the big esports, but its players are the poorest |date=13 August 2014 |website=[[The Daily Dot]] |access-date=2 May 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150518071207/http://www.dailydot.com/esports/dota-2-prize-distribution-players/ |archive-date=18 May 2015 }}</ref>

In 2015 it was estimated by SuperData Research, that the global esports industry generated revenue of around US$748.8 million that year. Asia is the leading esports market with over $321 million in revenue, with North America at around $224 million, and Europe at $172 million. For comparison, the rest of the world combines for approximately $29 million.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://fortune.com/2015/10/28/global-esports-revenues-nearing-2-billion/ |title=Global esports revenues are nearing 2 billion |first=John |last=Gaudiosi |website=[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]] |date=28 October 2015 |access-date=9 November 2015}}</ref> Global esports revenue is estimated to reach $1.9 billion by 2018. During the [[COVID-19 pandemic]], the video gaming industry bypassed many economic sectors by providing a means of compensating for the physical isolation imposed by the lockdown, transforming it into an increasingly important economic sector within the global economy.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Resolving Video Games and eSports Disputes: How Can WIPO Alternative Dispute Resolution Options Help? |url=https://www.wipo.int/wipo_magazine_digital/en/2023/article_0018.html |website=WIPO Magazine}}</ref>

===Gambling===
{{expand section|date=June 2018}}
{{main|Esports betting}}

Gambling on esports matches have historically been illegal or unregulated by major markets. This created a [[black market]] via virtual currency. In places where esports gambling is not officially recognized, the lack of regulation has resulted in match-fixing by players or third parties, and created issues with underage gambling due to the draw of video games. Some games allow bets in their [[in-game currency]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://kotaku.com/dota-2-now-lets-you-bet-in-game-currency-on-pro-tournam-1833502199|title=Dota 2 Now Lets You Bet In-Game Currency On Pro Tournaments|website=Kotaku|date=22 March 2019 |language=en-us|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref> while third-party gambling platforms will often take bets placed using virtual items earned in games.<ref name="wapost betting"/> In esports gambling, most bets and odds are structured in the same way as traditional sports. Most gambling sites offering the booker service allow users to bet based on the outcome of tournaments, matches or special esports titles. On the other hand, due to the nature of esports, there are numerous innovative ways to make bets, which are based on in-game milestones.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://venturebeat.com/2019/06/03/betting-is-esports-biggest-and-most-underappreciated-opportunity/|title=Betting is esports' biggest and most underappreciated opportunity|date=3 June 2019|website=VentureBeat|language=en-US|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref> For example, [[League of Legends|League of Legend]] bettors may place their money on which team/champion will take the "First Blood".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.lolbettingsites.com/lol-esports-bets/|title=LoL esports bets explained ➠ Best esports advice|website=LoLBettingSites.com|language=en-US|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref>

Esports gambling in the United States has been illegal under the federal [[Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act of 1992]] (PASPA). The Act prevented all but five states from allowing gambling on sporting events.<ref name="wapost betting"/> However, regulation of esports betting still depended on state law. Some betting houses in Nevada, where sports betting has been already exempted under PASPA, classify esports as non-competitive "other events" similar to the selection of the [[Heisman Trophy]] winner or [[NFL draft]] which are considered as legal.<ref name="wapost betting">{{cite news | title = Esports bookmaking? Globally, it's already a billion-dollar gambling industry |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/sports/breaking/ct-esports-bookmaking-20180406-story.html|first = Noah | last = Smith | date = 6 April 2018 | access-date = 8 June 2018 | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] }}</ref> Other companies established in the United States allow betting on esports to international users but are restricted to Americans. Nevada legalized esports gambling in June 2017, classifying esports along with competitive sports and dog racing.<ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.espn.com/chalk/story/_/id/19512317/chalk-nevada-governor-approves-esports-betting-bill | title = Nevada governor approves esports betting bill | first = Jacob | last = Wolf | date = 2 June 2017 | access-date = 8 June 2018 | work = [[ESPN]] }}</ref> With the [[Supreme Court of the United States]]'s ruling in ''[[Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association]]'' in May 2018, PASPA was recognized as unconstitutional, as the Court claimed that the federal government cannot limit states from regulating [[sports betting]]. This created the potential for legalized esports-based betting in the United States.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamesn.com/esports-betting | title = Esports betting may soon become legal in several American states | first = Ali | last= Jones | date = 17 May 2018 | access-date=8 June 2018 | work = [[PCGamesN]] }}</ref> However, New Jersey, the state at the center of the Supreme Court case, passed its bill to legalize sports gambling but restricted gambling on esports to only international competitions where most players are over 18 years of age.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://compete.kotaku.com/new-jersey-added-a-last-minute-esports-betting-ban-and-1826678155 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180610091914/https://compete.kotaku.com/new-jersey-added-a-last-minute-esports-betting-ban-and-1826678155 | archive-date = 10 June 2018 | title = New Jersey Added A Last-Minute Esports Betting Ban And No One Knows Why | first = Maddy | last= Myers | date = 8 June 2018 | access-date = 8 June 2018 | work = [[Kotaku]] }}</ref> Without PASPA, interstate gambling on esports would be still be limited by the [[Federal Wire Act]], preventing users from betting on national esports events outside of the state.<ref name="wapost betting"/>

In 2019, the countries where esports gambling is legal include the UK, New Zealand, Australia, China, Spain, Canada, South Korea, and Japan, and many of them are the international hosts for gaming tournaments.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gamopo.com/countries/|title=Esports Betting Laws & Country Restrictions 2019 {{!}} Gamopo Esports Hub|website=Gamopo.com|language=en-US|access-date=5 September 2019}}</ref> By the end of 2019, the state of [[New Jersey]] approved esports betting, just in time for the finals of the LoL Worlds Cup 2019 final match, which had over 4.000.000 spectators.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.esports.net/news/industry/new-jersey-allows-esports-betting-in-time-for-league-of-legends-final/|title=New Jersey Allows Esports Betting in Time for League of Legends Final|date=12 November 2019|website=Esports.net|language=en-US|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref>

The esports [[gambling industry]] has attracted criticism because of its target audience. As a large part of the esports audience is underage, governments and regulators have expressed skepticism regarding the market and the possibility of underage gambling. Additionally, gambling platforms have received criticism for their integration with the larger esports industry.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bräutigam |first1=Thiemo |title=Is it a problem that esports betting sites are sponsoring teams? – ARCHIVE – The Esports Observer |url=https://archive.esportsobserver.com/is-it-a-problem-that-esports-betting-sites-are-sponsoring-teams/ |website=Esports Observer |access-date=21 March 2022 |date=24 September 2015}}</ref> Esports platforms regularly sponsor professional esports teams, as happened with the contract between [[Betway]] and [[PSG.LGD]] team ([[Dota 2]]) in August 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://medium.com/instant-sponsor/betway-partners-with-psg-lgd-and-gains-control-over-team-branding-a447c8abb301|title=Betway Partners With PSG.LGD And Gains Control Over Team Branding|last=Kuchefski|first=Kathryn|date=14 August 2019|website=Medium|language=en|access-date=31 January 2020}}</ref>

===Data analytics and machine learning===
With the growing popularity of [[machine learning]] in data analytics,{{Citation needed|date=November 2018}} esports has been the focus of several software programs that analyze the plethora of game data available. Based on the huge number of matches played on a daily basis globally ([[League of Legends]] alone had a reported 100 million active monthly players worldwide in 2016<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.riftherald.com/2016/9/13/12865314/monthly-lol-players-2016-active-worldwide | title = Number of players of selected eSports games worldwide as of August 2017 (in million) | date = 13 September 2016 | access-date=12 August 2018 | work = [[Rift Herald]] }}</ref> and an average of 27 million League of Legends games played per day reported in 2014<ref>Sheer, Ian (27 January 2014). "Player Tally for 'League of Legends' Surges". Wsj.com. Archived from the original on 30 January 2014. Retrieved 31 January 2014.</ref>), these games can be used for applying big-data machine learning platforms. Several games make their data publicly available, so websites aggregate the data into easy-to-visualize graphs and statistics. In addition, several programs use machine learning tools to predict the win probability of a match based on various factors, such as team composition.<ref>{{cite arXiv | title = Win Prediction in Esports: Mixed-Rank Match Prediction in Multi-player Online Battle Arena Games | date = 17 November 2017 |eprint = 1711.06498|last1 = Hodge|first1 = Victoria|last2 = Devlin|first2 = Sam|last3 = Sephton|first3 = Nick|last4 = Block|first4 = Florian|last5 = Drachen|first5 = Anders|last6 = Cowling|first6 = Peter|class = cs.AI}}</ref> In 2018, the [[DotA]] team [[Team Liquid]] partnered with a software company to allow players and coaches to predict the team's success rate in each match and provide advice on what needs to be changed to improve performance.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.abs-cbn.com/sports/05/10/18/dota-analytics-big-data-meets-e-sports-in-software-giant-deal-with-team-liquid | title = 'DOTA analytics': Big data meets e-sports in software giant deal with Team Liquid | date = 10 May 2018 | access-date=12 August 2018 | work = [[ABS-CBN News]] }}</ref>

===Game cancellations===
As more esports competitions and leagues are run entirely or in portion by the video game publisher or developer for the game, the ongoing viability of that game's esports activities is tied to that company. In December 2018, Blizzard announced that it was reducing resources spent on the development of ''Heroes of the Storm'' and canceling its plans for tournaments in 2019. This caused several professional ''Heroes'' players and coaches to recognize that their career was no longer viable, and expressed outrage and disappointment at Blizzard's decision.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.engadget.com/2018/12/14/blizzard-ends-heroes-of-the-storm-esports/| title= Blizzard cancels 'Heroes of the Storm' eSports plans | first =Saqid | last = Shah | date = 14 December 2018 | access-date = 16 December 2018 | work = [[Engadget]] }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.polygon.com/2018/12/14/18141331/heroes-of-the-storm-canceled-hgc-blizzard-community | title = Heroes of the Storm pros vent sadness, anger after Blizzard kills game's esports future | first = Michael | last= McWhertor | date = 14 December 2018 | access-date = 16 December 2018 | work = [[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] }}</ref>

==Media coverage==
{{multiple image|image1=The International 2018 (30302304258).jpg|image2=The International 2018 (30302303908).jpg|footer=As with traditional sporting events, larger esport events, such as [[The International (Dota 2)|The International]], usually feature live pre- and post-game discussion by a panel of analysts (''top''), with in-match casting being done by [[play-by-play]] and [[color commentators]] (''bottom'').|width=250|direction=vertical|align=right}}

===News reporting===
The main medium for esports coverage is the [[Internet]]. In the mid-2010s, mainstream sports and news reporting websites, such as ''[[ESPN]]'', ''[[Yahoo!]]'', ''[[Sport1 (Germany)|Sport1]]'', ''[[Kicker (magazine)|Kicker]]'', and ''[[Aftonbladet]]'' started dedicated esports coverage.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dave |first1=Paresh |title=ESPN.com to cover e-sports with same 'rigor' as it does the big leagues |url=http://www.latimes.com/business/technology/la-fi-tn-espn-esports-20160113-story.html |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |access-date=13 July 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Yahoo Launches New Experience Dedicated to Esports |url=https://finance.yahoo.com/news/yahoo-launches-experience-dedicated-esports-050000022.html |website=Yahoo |access-date=13 July 2016}}</ref> Esports tournaments commonly use commentators or casters to provide live commentary of games in progress, similar to a traditional [[sports commentator]]. For popular casters, providing commentary for esports can be a full-time position by itself.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.polygon.com/features/2013/7/16/4503412/starcraft-commentators-tastosis |title=How two StarCraft commentators became stars |website=Polygon |author=Tracey Lien |date=16 July 2013 |access-date=11 September 2013}}</ref> Prominent casters for ''StarCraft II'' include [[Dan "Artosis" Stemkoski]] and [[Nick "Tasteless" Plott]]. However, the impact of [[COVID-19 pandemic]] affected how esports were covered in addition to the sports themselves. Notably, ''ESPN''{{'s}} dedicated esports coverage was shuttered in November 2020 as the network refocus on more traditional sports, though said they would still have some coverage of esports events.<ref>{{cite news | url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/video-games/esports/2021/02/16/espn-esports/ | title = The rise, fall and resonance of ESPN Esports | first = Noah | last = Smith | date = 16 February 2021 | access-date = 18 October 2021 | newspaper = [[The Washington Post]] }}</ref>
